item.title: DeepSeek Open-Sources DeepInfer, the Stack It Uses to Serve V4.1 Flash
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: DeepInfer is an Apache-2.0 inference framework built on vLLM that runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Nvidia SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, minus the KV cache and prefill/decode disaggregation pieces DeepSeek kept in-house.
item.content:encoded:
DeepSeek put its production inference stack on GitHub this week. The repo is called DeepInfer, it's Apache-2.0, and the company's one-line justification was that it's "sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs." Within days it had crossed 19,000 stars.

What's in it: a serving framework built mainly on vLLM with ideas borrowed from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, wired to DeepSeek's own kernel libraries (FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, DeepSelect and TileLang). The headline technique is a speculative-decoding scheme DeepSeek calls DSpark, which drafts up to five tokens ahead and verifies them on a confidence schedule. There's attention data-parallelism, balanced context parallelism, expert parallelism with load balancing for the MoE layers, an asynchronous batch scheduler turned on by default, and deterministic, batch-invariant sampling on Nvidia hardware. Structured output supports regex, JSON schema and EBNF grammars.

It runs exactly one model today, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with the 1017 checkpoint as the default. DeepSeek says future models will be added as they ship.

What's not in it is the more telling list. The README says the release is offline inference only and explicitly excludes the KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation, and data-parallel load balancing. Those three are most of what makes a large-scale serving deployment cheap. DeepSeek said back in 2025 that it wouldn't open its full engine as a single repo and would push components upstream instead, and DeepInfer is consistent with that: a very good single-node reference, not the thing actually running DeepSeek's API.

Hardware support is the other signal. The supported targets are Nvidia SM100 parts on CUDA 13 and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs on CANN 9.2. No Hopper, no consumer cards, and Ascend as a first-class target rather than an afterthought port. That matches where DeepSeek has said its compute is going, and it means the repo is more immediately useful to a Chinese cloud running Ascend than to a US startup with a rack of H100s.

The pricing context is why anyone outside the inference-kernel crowd cares. OpenRouter lists V4.1-Flash at $0.035 per million input tokens and $0.12 per million output. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra is listed at $10 and $50 for the same. That's not a like-for-like comparison, since the models aren't in the same class, but it's the gap DeepSeek is pointing at when it talks about lowering compute costs. The benchmarks DeepInfer publishes are prefill and decode Pareto curves measured on 4 and 64 SM100 GPUs respectively, with no absolute throughput numbers in the text, so treat the efficiency claims as directional until someone outside DeepSeek reproduces them.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Models Land on Google Cloud, the Last Hyperscaler Without Them
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are in private preview in Google Cloud's Model Garden, billed on the customer's existing Google invoice, with general availability promised in the coming weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Google Cloud now sells OpenAI. As of October 21, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are available in Model Garden as a private preview for selected enterprise customers, with OpenAI saying general availability is weeks away. Everyone else can fill in an interest form.

The models are positioned the way OpenAI positions them elsewhere: Astra for demanding coding, computer-use and research work, Sol as the cheaper option with most of Astra's capability, Luna for fast, high-volume routine tasks. Eligible customers can hit them through the API today and can point local Codex CLI and Codex Desktop sessions at Google's inference. Gemini for business and the Antigravity coding environment get them later. Zero Data Retention and Confidential Compute are listed as coming soon, which enterprise security teams will correctly read as "not yet."

The commercial mechanics matter more than the model list. Usage lands on the customer's existing Google Cloud invoice, draws down committed spend, and counts toward Flexible Savings Plans alongside Gemini and Anthropic usage. That's the whole pitch: a procurement team that already has a Google commit no longer needs a separate OpenAI contract to use GPT-6. Michael Gerstenhaber, VP of product management at Google Cloud, framed it as matching each workload to the right model. Google's own post goes further and claims it's now the only hyperscaler offering all three leading closed-source model families.

That claim is Google's, and it's narrowly true. Microsoft sells OpenAI and, more recently, Anthropic. AWS sells Anthropic and has carried OpenAI models since summer 2025. Neither sells Gemini.

GPT models were Azure-only for years because of Microsoft's investment. That exclusivity has been eroding for a while, first with AWS and now with Google, and Google was the obvious last stop. The more interesting question is what Microsoft gets out of the relationship now that its position as OpenAI's exclusive cloud is fully gone. The answer is probably the revenue share and the Azure consumption, which were always the point, but the marketing story is over.

For developers already on Vertex AI, the practical change is a model switch rather than a platform switch. For OpenAI, it's distribution into the accounts Google has been winning with Gemini. Watch the per-token pricing when GA lands. Google hasn't published any yet, and whether GPT-6 on Google costs the same as GPT-6 on OpenAI's own API will tell you who's subsidizing whom.

item.title: Tesla's Q3: Flat Revenue, Profit Down 43%, and Capex at Half of Plan
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Tesla booked $28.05 billion in revenue and $787 million in GAAP net income for the quarter, with AI and Optimus spending outrunning gross profit and nine-month capex at $13 billion against a full-year guide of more than $25 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Tesla's third quarter was flat on top and down hard underneath. Revenue came in at $28.05 billion, essentially unchanged from a year ago and in line with what Wall Street expected. GAAP net income fell 43% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share. Operating income dropped 56% to $718 million, a 2.6% operating margin, which the company attributes to AI and Optimus spending growing faster than gross profit.

The margin story is better than the profit story. Total gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% a year ago, and automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits climbed to 18.1% from 15.4%. Those credits, which propped up many a Tesla quarter, shrank 73% to $113 million. Services and other revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion. Energy generation and storage went the other way, down 16% to $2.88 billion even as deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh, which means pricing in that business is sliding.

Deliveries were 486,532, down about 2% year over year. Production was 464,391.

Tesla's explanation for the flat volume is new: battery availability "continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter." That's a supply constraint. Falling average selling prices are a demand signal. Both showing up in the same quarter doesn't quite add up, and the shareholder letter doesn't try to reconcile them.

Then there's capex. Tesla spent $4.73 billion in the quarter, down from $5.79 billion in Q2, bringing the nine-month total to $13.01 billion. Management guided the year to "more than $25 billion" and didn't update that number. Either the fourth quarter absorbs roughly $12 billion of spending, or a chunk of the 2026 plan (Optimus production lines, Cybercab capacity, the Terafab chip project) is quietly sliding into 2027. The lower spend is also why free cash flow looks respectable at $1.53 billion; it's still down 62% from a year ago.

Two line items below the operating line are worth noting. Tesla's bitcoin holdings produced a $288 million unrealized gain, and its SpaceX equity stake produced a $142 million unrealized loss, which together added about $146 million to GAAP net income. Strip them out and the quarter is thinner still.

On the autonomy side, the robotaxi fleet passed nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by quarter end, with Cybercab joining the Austin service about a month ago. FSD active subscriptions hit 1.74 million, up 67%, though that count includes upfront purchases, so it isn't a recurring-revenue number. The quarter reads as a company whose car business is treading water while its board and its CEO are busy on another question entirely: the SpaceX combination both companies' special committees are now studying.

item.title: A 2012 Test Account With 'Password1' Exposed 3,300 Welsh Children's Records
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The ICO reprimanded IT provider Ogi Networks and Data Cymru after a November 2024 ransomware attack walked in through a 12-year-old Active Directory account that nobody ever removed.
item.content:encoded:
Someone at Ogi Networks created an Active Directory account called Test2 on 13 January 2012. They gave it the password "Password1." Nobody deleted it. In November 2024, an attacker logged in with it, encrypted 182.7 GB across Data Cymru's file servers and SQL database, and walked out with 42 GB that included personal information on about 3,300 people, most of them children.

That's the whole story the UK Information Commissioner's Office told on October 20, when it published reprimands against both Ogi Networks Limited, the IT provider, and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, which trades as Data Cymru and is funded by the Welsh government. The stolen data came from a domain controller, a file server and an SQL server and covered two child and family projects.

The ICO ran the password through a strength tool. It rated "Password1" as very weak and estimated it could be cracked in under a second. The regulator's press release headline was blunt: "'Password1' is not an appropriate password." David Doodson, the ICO's head of investigations, said organisations should remove accounts that are no longer required and block weak, commonly used passwords. Ogi said it accepted the findings and had acted on them.

The ICO found both organisations breached UK GDPR but put more of the fault on Ogi, which created the account, never removed it, and never reviewed local administrator accounts after initial setup. Neither got a fine. Reprimands only.

That's the part worth sitting with. A public body's IT provider left a default-password account live for twelve years, it led to the theft of children's data, and the consequence is a published letter. The ICO has said for a couple of years that it prefers reprimands over fines for public-sector bodies so money isn't pulled from services. Ogi is a private company, though, and the same leniency applied. Since the attack, Ogi has tightened account access controls and the two organisations have signed a compliant data processing contract, which the reprimand notes they didn't have before.

The practical takeaway is the one every audit framework already has in it and nobody enjoys doing: pull your Active Directory for accounts with no login in a year, accounts with "test" in the name, and accounts created before your current staff joined. Then check which of them still have a password that would fail a 2012 complexity policy. Ogi's did, and the ICO's reprimand will sit on the first page of search results for both companies for years.

item.title: FoxIO Publishes PoC for QPACK Flaws That Crash 7 of 10 HTTP/3 Servers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: FoxIO's Header Accordions research shows tiny compressed header batches expanding thousands of times in memory on quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, lsquic and Bun, with fixes out for three stacks and Bun, hyperium h3 and aioquic still open.
item.content:encoded:
Under 10 MiB of traffic across 50 connections. That's what it took in FoxIO's proof-of-concept to push an HTTP/3 server's container to its 5 GiB memory cap in about a second. The write-up, titled Header Accordions, went public on October 20 along with working exploit code, and it found the same flaw class in seven of the ten HTTP/3 implementations the firm tested.

The bug is in how QPACK, HTTP/3's header compression scheme, gets enforced. Most stacks cap the compressed size of a header block on the wire. Fewer cap what that block expands into, or they apply the limit only after the whole thing has been decoded into memory. FoxIO's first technique exploits that gap directly: on quic-go at default settings, a 1 MB batch unpacked into roughly 160,000 header fields and around 15 MB of resident memory, about 17x amplification. quic-go's own advisory puts the ceiling closer to 50x.

The second technique is nastier. The attacker stores a single header entry of about 4 KB in the dynamic table, then references it over and over with one-byte indexed references. Every reference makes the server rebuild the full entry. FoxIO measured roughly 4,000x amplification on Bun and 600 to 1,800x on lsquic. Bun has an extra problem on top: a running-total counter overflows past 2 GB and the decoder spins forever, so a single stream of about 516 KB pins a core at 100%.

This is denial of service, not code execution. FoxIO reports no data exposure and no evidence of in-the-wild use.

Patch status is mixed. quic-go fixed it in 0.57.0 (CVE-2025-64702), Cloudflare's quiche in 0.29.3 (CVE-2026-12523), and lsquic in 4.9.0 back in July by capping the unpacked header sets held per stream, though lsquic never issued a CVE. Wireshark picked up CVE-2025-13945 for a dissector crash, which matters for anyone running packet capture on untrusted traffic but isn't a server-side issue. Bun, hyperium's h3 crate, and aioquic (which mitmproxy depends on) have no fix as of FoxIO's publication. IIS, Envoy, ngtcp2/nghttp3 and Google's quiche were not affected because they count unpacked headers as they decode.

If you run one of the unpatched stacks: don't expose Bun's HTTP/3 server to the internet, start mitmproxy with http3 disabled, and set max_field_section_size on h3. If you run one of the patched ones, this is a plain upgrade. And if you're behind a CDN that terminates HTTP/3 for you, this is a good week to ask which stack they're running.

item.title: Node.js Patches Brotli RCE Reachable Through fetch() in 22, 24 and 26
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in Node's bundled Brotli decoder, fixed in 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1, and any app that decompresses br responses or request bodies is in scope.
item.content:encoded:
Ten CVEs, three release lines, one Wednesday. The Node.js project shipped 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, and the one to care about is CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled into Node itself. The project rates it High and says plainly that it permits remote code execution.

What makes this worse than a typical decoder bug is how little an app has to do to reach it. Node's built-in fetch() transparently decompresses responses tagged Content-Encoding: br. Express 5's body parser decompresses br request bodies by default. So a service that never imports zlib, never calls brotliDecompress, and never thinks about compression can still hand attacker-controlled bytes to the vulnerable code, either by fetching a hostile URL or by accepting a crafted POST.

Exploitation hasn't been reported. The advisory says nothing about attacks in the wild, no CVSS score is published yet, and the bug isn't on CISA's KEV list. That's today. Decoder memory-corruption bugs with a clear trigger path tend not to stay theoretical.

The other three High-rated fixes are all about identity. CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483 are TLS hostname-verification bypasses (one triggered when a hostname loosely resolves to an IP, the other when an IP is written in fullwidth Unicode digits), and CVE-2026-105482 is a dns.resolve bug that truncates names containing a NUL byte. Individually they're edge cases. Together they're the kind of thing that turns a certificate check into a suggestion. Three Medium and three Low issues round out the ten, including a randomUUID() entropy-cache bug that makes processes built from startup snapshots or single-executable applications repeat values they should never repeat.

If you're on Node 20 or 25, there's no patch coming. Both lines are end-of-life, and the project's position is that EOL versions are always affected by security releases. That's a bigger population than it sounds. Node 20 was the LTS line a lot of production fleets standardized on, and a fair number of them haven't moved.

Update to the fixed version on your line. If you can't do it today, the narrower mitigations are to strip br from the Accept-Encoding header on outbound fetch() calls and disable br inflation in body parsers until you can. Then go find out which of your containers are still pinned to node:20.

item.title: PHP2Shell: Two 9.2 RCE Bugs Hit Every PHP Since 5.4, Patch Lands Today
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: PHP ships an out-of-cycle fix at 14:00 UTC for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 after exploit code leaked a day early and Cloudflare reported the first attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Every web server running PHP 5.4 or later is exposed to a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution bugs, and the only real fix arrives at 14:00 UTC today. PHP's security team posted the advance notice on Monday, rating both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 at CVSS v4.0 9.2 and promising version details with the release. By Tuesday night the embargo had collapsed. Someone leaked a screenshot of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, credited to Calif.IO, with a banner claiming it works against every PHP release from 5.4.0 onward.

watchTowr, which had been working under the original embargo, said everyone was supposed to wait until Thursday. The PHP team pulled the release forward to Wednesday instead. watchTowr also says it independently reproduced CVE-2026-109618, which is about as strong a confirmation as you'll get before the patch drops.

The attack surface appears to be multipart form parsing. PHP processes multipart/form-data request bodies before any application code runs, which is why PHP core developers have been blunt that configuration won't save you. Core developer Gina Peter Banyard called patching the only mitigation, and 8.6 release manager Joe Ferguson said flatly that ini settings won't help. Disabling session upload progress does nothing against this.

Exploitation has started. Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said the company was seeing early attacks emerging, and Sansec's timeline puts Cloudflare's first observation at 07:43 UTC on Wednesday, hours before the patch. Nobody has published indicators yet. Sansec, which watches e-commerce platforms like Magento, Shopware, and WooCommerce, expects mass scanning within 15 minutes of the fix going public, because the diff will tell attackers exactly where to aim.

Fixes are coming only for supported branches: 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. Pre-release reporting from Kevin Beaumont points to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 as the fixed builds, but confirm against php.net once the release is live. PHP 8.1 and everything older is end-of-life and gets nothing official. One estimate puts the count of internet-facing EOL PHP hosts near 884,000. Distribution vendors will backport for the enterprise Linux branches they still support, so check your distro's advisory rather than assuming you're stuck.

If you can't patch in the next few hours, the stopgaps are ugly but real. Block multipart/form-data at nginx or Apache, which also breaks file uploads. Put the origin behind a WAF (Cloudflare says its managed rules cover the known vectors, free tier included) and lock origin access to the WAF's IP ranges so attackers can't go around it. Or take the site read-only by rejecting anything that isn't GET or HEAD. CERT-EU went further and told members to isolate internet-facing PHP applications until fixed.

One warning: exploit code is circulating on forums and GitHub, and almost none of it is verified. Some of it will be malware aimed at defenders who download it to test. Wait for the official diff.

item.title: eMudhra's CA Keys Could Be Computed From Public Certs. Browsers Pulled Them
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were generated with so little randomness that a researcher recovered every private key in under a second, forcing Chrome, Firefox, Apple, and Microsoft to block them.
item.content:encoded:
Scott Helme recovered all eight private keys in less than a second. He didn't steal them. He computed them from the public certificates, because eMudhra's April 2025 key generation ceremony produced keys with so little entropy that the math falls apart on inspection. Anyone who did the same work could have minted a certificate for any domain on the internet, and Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Windows would have trusted it.

The report came in on Friday, October 17, from a researcher Mozilla credits only as Wayne. Chrome's Root Program had a CRLSet block live within an hour and forty minutes. Mozilla's team recovered the keys themselves within two hours of being notified and had OneCRL pushed by late evening. Apple blocked the certificates Sunday, Android devices got a block through Play Services Sunday night, and Microsoft followed Monday. Google and Mozilla published their statements Monday too. That's a fast, coordinated response, and it deserves credit.

The eight certificates break down as six TLS intermediates (DV, OV, and EV, each in a G3B and G3C variant) chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, plus two code-signing intermediates. Each also exists as a Sectigo cross-signed copy with the same public key, which is why Chrome blocked by key rather than by certificate. Chrome didn't block the code-signing pair because its TLS verifier won't build a path through a code-signing-restricted intermediate anyway.

eMudhra's account, published Tuesday to the Bombay Stock Exchange, is that the ceremony used FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSMs and a flaw in a key wrap/unwrap step produced a second, weak set of keys alongside the intended strong ones. The weak set is what got published to root stores. The company says its infrastructure wasn't breached, that only one of the eight was ever deployed in production, that none issued end-entity certificates, and that global TLS is about 1% of its revenue. Its shares dropped roughly 20% in Mumbai anyway.

Here's the problem with the reassurance. No certificate chaining to the six TLS intermediates appears in Certificate Transparency logs before Chrome's block, which is good. But CT only records what's logged, and a forged certificate used in a targeted interception would have no reason to be logged. Nobody can say whether these keys were abused. eMudhra is also still determining the root cause of a flaw it has already explained, which reads like the explanation arrived before the investigation did.

The browser side is handled for you. The rest of your stack isn't. Go binaries, Python's certifi bundle, Node.js, and most non-browser TLS clients don't check revocation and will trust these chains until their root bundles or code change. Go shipped 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 to reject the eight keys, which requires rebuilding; Go 1.25 and older get nothing. Node's fix is a draft PR. Cloudflare pushed updated WARP, 1.1.1.1, and cloudflared clients. Chrome removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 entirely in root store version 43, expected to reach devices around October 27, and anyone with a certificate under that root needs a new chain before then.

If you run anything that pins a root bundle, audit it this week.

item.title: Qilin and Inc Ransomware Walk Through a GlobalProtect Bug Patched in May
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Unit 42 says at least two ransomware crews are using CVE-2026-0257, an authentication override cookie flaw in PAN-OS GlobalProtect, to open VPN sessions without credentials and bypass MFA on their way to vCenter.
item.content:encoded:
The bug was rated medium when Palo Alto Networks disclosed it on May 13. Four days later Rapid7 saw attackers using it against customer firewalls. Five months on, Palo Alto's own Unit 42 team has updated its threat brief to say Qilin and Inc ransomware affiliates are among the groups exploiting it, and ReliaQuest adds Settra to the list. The flaw is CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass in GlobalProtect portals and gateways, and the fix has been available since the day it was disclosed.

The mechanics are embarrassing in the way VPN bugs usually are. GlobalProtect's authentication override feature issues a cookie so users don't have to re-authenticate for a set period. The firewall trusted that cookie without properly validating its integrity, so a remote attacker with no credentials could forge one and establish a VPN session. MFA never comes into it because the cookie says you already passed. Palo Alto now scores it CVSS 4.0 7.8 with exploit maturity marked as attacked, and its advisory asks for the highest urgency.

What the crews do after they're in is textbook, which is the point. Unit 42 describes attackers using legitimate IT management tools to look around and move laterally, then credential and data theft, then ransomware. In one case the intruders went from the VPN gateway to the vCenter appliance, disabled security controls on the ESXi hosts, and ran a custom tool against the domain controller's virtual disk to pull credentials offline. Some chained in the old Veeam bug, CVE-2023-27532. ReliaQuest found Cobalt Strike, BloodHound, and SharpHound in its cases. Healthcare, education, government, and energy have all taken hits.

Exposure requires a specific setup: a GlobalProtect portal or gateway with authentication override cookies enabled, plus a particular certificate configuration. That's a real limiter and probably why the initial severity was low. It's also a common enough configuration that two separate ransomware operations built playbooks around it.

Fixed builds span four PAN-OS branches. On 12.1 you need 12.1.4-h6 or 12.1.7; on 11.2, 11.2.4-h17, 11.2.7-h14, 11.2.10-h7, or 11.2.12; on 11.1, 11.1.4-h33, 11.1.6-h32, 11.1.7-h6, 11.1.10-h25, 11.1.13-h5, or 11.1.15; on 10.2, 10.2.7-h34, 10.2.10-h36, 10.2.13-h21, 10.2.16-h7, or 10.2.18-h6. Prisma Access needs 11.2.7-h13 or 10.2.10-h36. Cloud NGFW and Panorama aren't affected. If you can't patch, use a dedicated certificate for authentication override cookies or turn the override options off entirely in the portal and gateway config.

Patching isn't the whole job. ReliaQuest's warning is that access established before remediation survives it. Terminate every active GlobalProtect session after you upgrade, then go through the connection logs for anything you don't recognize. Unit 42 specifically flags sessions from hosts named "kali," which tells you how little effort some of these operators bother with. ReliaQuest expects the exploitation to run at least another three months, because the install base that hasn't patched in five months isn't going to start now.

item.title: Salesforce Pays $5.66B for Braze to Fix the Marketing Cloud It Already Owns
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Braze shareholders get $47.50 a share in cash, Braze keeps its brand and CEO, and the deal won't close before Salesforce's next fiscal year.
item.content:encoded:
$47.50 a share, all cash, about $5.66 billion in enterprise value. That's what Salesforce agreed Monday to pay for Braze, the customer engagement platform that sends the push notifications, in-app messages, SMS, WhatsApp, and email that brands like Instacart, Venmo, Canva, and Dairy Queen fire at their customers. Braze stock jumped around 50% on the news, which tells you roughly how far below that price it had been trading.

Salesforce already sells this. Marketing Cloud has been in the portfolio since the ExactTarget deal in 2013, and the company has spent a decade bolting acquisitions onto it. Buying Braze is an admission that the real-time, event-driven side of the product never caught up with the specialists. Braze was built on a streaming architecture that reacts to what a user just did inside an app, and that's precisely the capability Salesforce needs if Agentforce is going to do anything useful in consumer marketing beyond drafting copy.

The official framing is that Braze complements all four layers of the Salesforce stack: Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce. Strip the branding and it means Braze's decisioning engine gets wired to Salesforce's customer data and agent layer. Braze will keep its name and CEO Bill Magnuson stays on with his leadership team. It has about 2,770 customers and 15 offices.

The price is steep by Salesforce's own numbers. The company said it's paying roughly five times Braze's expected fiscal 2028 revenue, and outside estimates put it near eight times trailing revenue. Salesforce says it expects the deal to add to growth but dilute profitability in the near term, and that it doesn't need debt to fund it. Fiscal 2027 guidance is unchanged. The deal closes in fiscal 2028, which starts in February, and only after Braze shareholders and regulators sign off.

Regulators are the open question. Salesforce and Braze are two of the larger vendors of brand-to-consumer messaging, and consolidation in martech has gone mostly unchallenged for years. This is a big enough check, in a category with few remaining independents, that someone in Washington or Brussels may at least ask.

For teams running Braze today, nothing changes for at least four months. After that, expect the Salesforce sales motion to show up in your renewal conversation.

item.title: SpaceX and Tesla Boards Form Merger Committees as SpaceX Posts a $4.4B Quarter
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Musk confirmed on SpaceX's first earnings call as a public company that independent directors at both firms are studying a combination he isn't allowed to negotiate, while SpaceX's AI compute business grew ninefold.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk spent part of SpaceX's first earnings call as a public company explaining why he can't be in the room. Both the SpaceX and Tesla boards have formed special committees of independent directors to study a merger, he said Tuesday, and because he's a conflicted party under securities rules, he isn't on either one and isn't part of the talks. He called the whole thing an odd Kabuki dance. He also said he thinks it's a good idea.

The committees exist because shareholders asked for them. No terms have been agreed, Musk said, and there's no guarantee any will be. A deal would need approval from a majority of all Tesla shares outstanding, not just the shares that vote, which he described as quite a high hurdle. Anyone treating the merger as a certainty is overstating it, in his words. The market shrugged at the caveats: SpaceX shares rose between 5% and 8% after hours depending on which report you read.

The numbers underneath the call explain why the question keeps coming up. SpaceX booked $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 161% from a year ago, and a $4.4 billion profit against a $1.1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. Starlink did $5.2 billion of that, up 69%, on 13.6 million consumer subscribers, though average monthly revenue per subscriber slipped to $69 from $83 as the service pushes into cheaper markets.

The bigger story is the line item that didn't exist at this scale a year ago. SpaceX's AI unit, built on the xAI acquisition it closed in February and has since renamed SpaceXSI, booked $7.6 billion in the quarter, more than nine times the prior year. Most of that is renting compute to other labs. Anthropic has agreed to pay nearly $45 billion over three years, and Google is paying $920 million a month through mid-2029. SpaceX is now, by revenue, as much a data center landlord as a launch company.

That's also the merger logic Musk offered: AI software, chip design, robotics, and connectivity overlap between the two companies. Tesla already put about $2 billion into a SpaceX AI subsidiary in January. The pieces are being arranged in public, one related-party transaction at a time, and the special committees are the governance answer to a question investors have been asking since the SpaceX IPO.

What the committees can't change is the arithmetic of a majority-of-all-outstanding vote at Tesla, where a large retail base and index funds that often abstain make any threshold hard. Musk knows this, which is probably why he said it out loud.

item.title: Anthropic Is Near a Second $45B Nscale Deal. Its Compute Tab Could Hit $750B
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Bloomberg and CNBC report a second 460 MW West Virginia deal is days from signing, while the Journal's read of Anthropic's draft IPO filing shows $450 billion in noncancelable cloud commitments already on the books.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is close to signing a second roughly $45 billion compute deal with Nscale, according to Bloomberg and CNBC, covering another 460-megawatt building at the Monarch campus in West Virginia. The first Monarch deal, struck in August, was about the same size. If this one closes in the coming days as reported, a single data center operator with an unfinished IPO will be holding around $90 billion of Anthropic's forward spending.

Neither company has commented, and the reporting hedges that terms could still change. Treat it as likely, not done.

The deal matters less on its own than as a data point in a number the Wall Street Journal pulled from Anthropic's draft IPO prospectus this week. The filing shows roughly $450 billion in noncancelable cloud commitments over the next decade: about $111 billion to Google Cloud, $110 billion to Amazon Web Services, and $31 billion to Microsoft, with the rest spread across other providers. Add the deals still being negotiated, Nscale among them, and the Journal's total reaches as much as $750 billion. For scale, SpaceX disclosed Tuesday that Anthropic alone has agreed to pay it nearly $45 billion over three years for compute.

The same filing explains why Anthropic can contemplate that. Revenue for the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier, and against full-year 2025 revenue of $4.6 billion. The headline net loss of $80.7 billion for the half is mostly an accounting artifact: about $72 billion of it comes from revaluing convertible notes and other instruments as the company's valuation rose. Actual cash burn was closer to $9 billion in six months, which is still more than Anthropic spent in all of 2025. The IPO is reportedly targeting a valuation of up to $2 trillion.

Here's the skeptical read. Noncancelable means noncancelable. These are decade-long obligations priced against a revenue curve that has gone from one billion to sixteen billion in a year and is assumed to keep bending upward. The commitments are also concentrated in a small number of counterparties, several of which (Amazon, Google) are also investors and competitors, and one of which (Nscale) has had a rough few months. Microsoft walked away from anchoring Nscale's Loughton site in the UK over grid delays and reportedly from Monarch itself shortly after signing a letter of intent. Investors have pushed back on Nscale's roughly $30 billion IPO valuation.

Whether that's a problem depends entirely on whether demand holds. Anthropic is betting $450 billion to $750 billion that it does. The filing will be public soon enough, and the commitments footnote is the first thing worth reading.

item.title: Stolen ConnectWise Backup Secret Opened 300+ Microsoft 365 Tenants
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A compromised Microsoft 365 app secret for ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) let an attacker into hundreds of customer tenants, and ConnectWise has shut off Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management while it investigates.
item.content:encoded:
If you're an MSP, the app you trusted to back up your clients' Microsoft 365 data has been used to break into them. ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service, the product it picked up when it bought SkyKick, on October 17 after an attacker got hold of a Microsoft 365 API secret belonging to the app and used it to sign into customer tenants.

Huntress raised the alarm first. Its initial count was 162 tenants with confirmed unauthorized sign-ins as of October 16. A later update put the number at almost 1,000 Entra tenants seeing sign-in attempts from the attacker's infrastructure, with more than 300 of them succeeding.

The worrying part is what the attacker did once inside. In one partner tenant, the ConnectWise Cloud Management MS Teams app added itself to the Global Administrator role, then planted fresh client secrets on two other applications. One of those was a Huntress app unique to that partner. That's textbook persistence: even after ConnectWise kills its own apps, the attacker still holds working credentials on things you didn't think to check.

Huntress says password spraying started around October 13 and 14, with the privilege grab happening early on October 15 UTC. It also saw a separate, targeted wave against 16 tenants in policy, national security, trade and critical-minerals sectors, which reads a lot more like espionage than smash-and-grab. ConnectWise says it "cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time," and nobody else has named a group yet.

ConnectWise's own messaging has leaned on reassurance. The company says existing backup archives remain encrypted and isolated, and that the outage on its own doesn't mean an MSP or client was compromised. Both may be true. But ConnectWise also admits it has no visibility into the tenants its apps had access to, which puts the cleanup squarely on partners. And Huntress points out that Microsoft Graph directory reads don't leave an audit trail, so a clean-looking sign-in log isn't proof of a clean tenant.

Here's the to-do list. Disable (don't delete) every ConnectWise and SkyKick service principal, including the Cloud Backup app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, and leave them off until ConnectWise confirms credentials are rotated. Audit client secrets and certificates on every enterprise app and app registration added since October 13 and remove anything you didn't create. Look for ConnectWise apps holding privileged directory roles, block the 144.172.64.0/24 addresses Huntress published, and remember that tokens issued before you disabled anything can stay valid until they expire.

Third-party apps with tenant-wide Graph permissions are effectively the new domain admin, and most shops still don't inventory them. If this week sends you hunting through Enterprise Applications for the first time, you're not alone.

item.title: Plex2Shell: Unpatched Plex Servers Are Being Hijacked to Mine Monero
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A public exploit for a four-bug Plex Media Server chain (CVE-2026-96652, -96654, -96655, -96656) was weaponized within a day, and anyone still on 1.43.2 or earlier is exposed to unauthenticated code execution.
item.content:encoded:
It took about a day. A researcher published a full write-up and proof-of-concept for "Plex2Shell" on October 16, and by October 17 a honeypot was catching attackers using it to drop cryptominers on Plex Media Server.

Plex2Shell chains four bugs: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656. Reporting describes them as a pair of server-side request forgery flaws (one in the transcoder), a URL injection in plugin calls, and an arbitrary file write that executes when loaded. Strung together, they give an unauthenticated attacker code execution on an internet-exposed server with whatever privileges the Plex service runs under.

The fix isn't new. The bugs were reported to Plex on July 27, confirmed with a bounty on August 4, and patched on September 1. Plex's forum advisory covers Media Server 1.43.2 and earlier and told owners to update "without delay." Security reporting puts the first safe build at 1.43.3.10861.

Payloads so far are boring but telling: an XMRig-based Monero miner and a proxy tool called myawesomeproxy, which turns your home connection into someone else's exit node. That second one is the bigger problem. Residential proxies are exactly what credential stuffers and fraud crews pay for, and your IP is the one that shows up in the logs.

Plex is a weird category of software. It's consumer-grade, but plenty of it runs on NAS boxes and homelab servers sitting next to real work data, often with port 32400 forwarded straight to the internet for remote streaming. And NAS package managers don't always pull Plex updates automatically, which Plex itself warned about. Six weeks of patch availability means nothing if the update never reached the box.

Check your version in Settings, then General. If it's 1.43.2 or older, update now, and if it was exposed while unpatched, look for unfamiliar processes, high CPU and new files in the Plex plug-in directories before you assume you got lucky. CISA hasn't added these CVEs to KEV, but with public code and confirmed in-the-wild use, that's a formality.

item.title: Disney Is Hiring Most of Bankrupt Character.AI's Staff, Not Its Chatbots
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A bankruptcy filing shows Disney offering jobs to at least 60 Character.AI employees, worth about $60 million a year in pay, alongside a $20 million stalking-horse bid for a slice of the startup's technology.
item.content:encoded:
Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 last week. Now we know who gets the people. According to a court filing first reported by Bloomberg, Disney has agreed to offer jobs to at least 60 Character.AI employees, most of the company's remaining workforce, with an estimated $60 million in combined annual compensation. The filing says the "vast majority" of those offered have already accepted.

Disney is also the stalking-horse bidder for some of the company's assets at $20 million. Reporting on the term sheet describes a non-exclusive, perpetual license to code behind Character.AI's training, safety and serving systems, plus a handful of patents. What it reportedly doesn't include matters more: user data, conversation logs, training data, finished models, the brand and the consumer app. Rival bids can still come in before a proposed auction in late November, and a bankruptcy judge has to sign off.

So Disney is buying a team and an inference stack, not a chatbot company. That fits. Karandeep Anand, Character.AI's former CEO, recently became Disney's first CTO, and a studio sitting on the most valuable character IP on the planet has obvious reasons to want people who know how to run millions of persona conversations cheaply.

It also tells you what Disney didn't want. Character.AI's filing blames high costs along with "potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement." The company faces a wrongful-death lawsuit over a teenager's suicide and a Texas attorney general investigation into child safety. Leaving the user data and the consumer product behind is a clean way to keep that baggage out of a family-entertainment brand.

This is the second time Character.AI's talent has been peeled off without a traditional acquisition. In 2024, Google paid to license its technology and rehired founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. The pattern is getting familiar across AI: the people and the code walk out the door, while the liabilities stay with the shell.

The open question is what happens to the users still chatting with Character.AI bots today. Nothing in the filing commits anyone to keeping the app running.

item.title: DHS Orders DeepSeek, and Anything Built on It, Off Federal Civilian IT
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A Homeland Security order published in today's Federal Register uses the 2018 supply chain security law to bar DeepSeek products from civilian agency purchases and force removal of DeepSeek and third-party tools built on its models.
item.content:encoded:
The federal government just moved past "please don't use DeepSeek" to a binding order. A notice published in the Federal Register on October 20 (document 2026-21447) records an order from the Secretary of Homeland Security that excludes products and services from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. and its affiliates from federal civilian agency procurements, and requires agencies to rip out what they already have.

The clause that matters is the second one. Removal doesn't stop at DeepSeek's own apps and API. It also covers third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations. That's a much wider net, because DeepSeek's open-weight models have been folded into a lot of software that doesn't put the name on the box.

The legal hook is the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (41 U.S.C. 1321-1328). Under FASCSA, the interagency Federal Acquisition Security Council reviews a vendor and recommends action, and then DHS, the Pentagon or the Director of National Intelligence issues an order for its slice of government. DHS covers civilian agencies, so this one doesn't directly bind the Defense Department or the intelligence community. The notice says the order followed review of the council's recommendation "and affiliated evidence," without spelling out what that evidence is.

It's only the second public FASCSA order we know of. The first, from ODNI in September 2025, targeted Swiss backup vendor Acronis. Going after a model maker is a different kind of target, and the public notice leaves the hardest question unanswered: does an open-weight DeepSeek model, downloaded and run on an agency's own air-gapped hardware, count as a DeepSeek product? The order text itself sits in scanned pages, and the summary doesn't say.

That ambiguity is the real burden here. Agencies now have to find every tool, plug-in and vendor platform with a DeepSeek model somewhere in the stack, and plenty of software vendors don't disclose which base models they fine-tuned. Expect a round of contractor questionnaires asking exactly that.

If you sell software to civilian agencies, start building that answer now. A model bill of materials was a nice-to-have last week. For federal sales, it isn't anymore.

item.title: ClickFix Crews Are Abusing a Signed Siemens App to Sideload Malware
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Siemens says CVE-2026-110936, a DLL sideloading flaw in Software Center 3.5.8.7 fixed in 4.0.9.8, is being exploited by the Romulus ClickFix operation to run malware behind a genuinely signed Siemens executable.
item.content:encoded:
The executable is real, it's signed by Siemens, and it hasn't been touched. That's the whole trick. Attackers running ClickFix campaigns are dropping a genuine copy of Siemens Software Center next to a malicious DLL called archive.dll, and the signed program loads it without checking.

Siemens tracks the bug as CVE-2026-110936 in advisory SSA-580366, scored 8.4 under CVSS 4.0. Software Center 3.5.8.7, the current release when the advisory went out on October 15, loads helper files from its own folder without verifying them. Version 4.0.9.8 fixes it, and existing installs pick up the update automatically the next time they launch. Siemens updated the advisory on October 17 and posted an active-exploitation notice on October 19. Huntress researcher Jose Oregon reported the flaw.

Siemens is clear that none of its systems or update channels were breached. The malicious installer, AllMyBasic.msi, circulates outside official channels and has been tied to Romulus, a ClickFix delivery backend that Forescout's Vedere Labs uncovered during an incident investigation. Forescout describes it as reusable infrastructure rather than a single malware server, and nobody has named the operator.

The lure end is grim in a very 2026 way. The Hacker News, citing Huntress, reports that some victims came in through malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs that pointed them at fake ClickFix pages. From there it's the usual routine: paste a PowerShell command, an MSI drops, the signed Siemens binary launches and pulls in the attacker's DLL. Payloads reported so far include LegionLoader, which grabs data from Chrome, and a remote access trojan.

For defenders, hash-based blocking is useless here because the executable is legitimate. Hunt for SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe running out of AppData\Local\Programs, especially right after msiexec, and on machines with no business reason to have Siemens industrial software at all. If you do run Software Center, open it so the 4.0.9.8 update applies.

This is also a decent argument for application control that cares about path and parent process, not just a valid signature. Signed-binary sideloading isn't new, and it keeps working because "is it signed?" is still the question too many tools stop at.

item.title: China-Linked Armory Castle Hit BeyondTrust Remote Support as a Zero-Day
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: BeyondTrust's CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS 9.3) was exploited from August 29 by a China-nexus group Mandiant tracks as Armory Castle, and CISA's federal patch deadline is today.
item.content:encoded:
Attackers had root on BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances for more than a month before anyone knew the bug existed. BeyondTrust's advisory BT26-05, published October 15, covers CVE-2026-102764, a flaw in how an internal messaging component validates where messages come from. It lets an unauthenticated remote attacker perform file operations on the appliance. BeyondTrust scores it 9.3 under CVSS 4.0.

Every Remote Support version up to and including 26.2.3 is affected. The BT26-05-RS patch applies to 24.3.1 through 26.2.3, so anyone running something older has to upgrade first and then patch. SaaS customers were patched by October 9. Self-hosted appliances without automatic updates are on you.

BeyondTrust says the first exploitation it can find dates to August 29, against one BeyondTrust-hosted instance and one self-hosted appliance. Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group attribute the activity to Armory Castle, the China-nexus espionage cluster formerly tracked as UNC5221 (CrowdStrike calls it Warp Panda). That's the same crew with a long résumé of edge-device zero-days, Ivanti most famously.

The post-exploitation playbook is what should worry you. According to Mandiant, the attackers escalated to root, dropped a PHP webshell called Sawfly for encrypted command and control, ran a SOCKS5 tunneler called Bareclaw, harvested credentials, wiped system and web server logs, and then used stolen admin credentials to move into downstream systems. They also pulled internal documents out through Remote Support's own file transfer feature.

Think about what a remote support appliance actually is: a box that holds privileged access to a large share of your endpoints, by design. Owning it is close to owning the help desk. That's why this one matters more than its file-operations description suggests.

CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 16 and gave federal agencies until today, October 19, to remediate. A three-day window tells you how seriously the agency is taking it.

If you run self-hosted Remote Support, confirm BT26-05-RS is applied, then assume compromise if the appliance was internet-facing between late August and your patch date. Rotate any credentials stored in or used through it, check for missing or truncated logs (log deletion was part of the playbook), and hunt for the Sawfly and Bareclaw indicators Mandiant published.

item.title: PEERSTITCH: One Hacked FortiManager Exposed 500+ FortiGates at a Telecom MSP
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Unit 42 traced a two-year intrusion that chained FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575) and FortiOS CVE-2025-61624 into a memory-only implant hiding inside FortiGate's own logging and VPN daemons.
item.content:encoded:
A single FortiManager box handed attackers the configurations, keys and credentials for more than 500 FortiGate firewalls. That's the core finding in Palo Alto Networks Unit 42's October 14 write-up on PEERSTITCH, an implant it found at a telecommunications managed service provider. Many of those firewalls sat in front of the MSP's customers, not the MSP itself.

The intrusion started back in September 2024 with CVE-2024-47575, the FortiJump bug that gave unauthenticated command execution on FortiManager and was widely exploited that fall. After a long dwell period, the attackers came back for the firewalls. They used CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS path traversal flaw (Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-122) that lets an authenticated read-write admin write or delete arbitrary files, to get root on the underlying OS.

Then came PEERSTITCH. It's an ARM64 Linux injector that ptrace-attaches to two legitimate FortiGate processes, miglogd (logging) and iked (IPsec key exchange), and patches their memory. There's no binary left on disk, no listening port, and no direct outbound connection to flag. Unit 42 also found the attackers abusing an ACME DNS-01 challenge path in Apache's mod_md to run commands, which ended in an SSH reverse shell.

Unit 42 tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954, overlapping with what Mandiant calls UNC5820, and says parts of the activity resemble suspected nation-state intrusions. It stops short of naming a country, and so will we.

Here's the uncomfortable part. CVE-2025-61624 is scored medium, 5.4 by Fortinet and 6.5 by NVD, because it needs admin credentials. That math falls apart when an attacker already stole every admin credential from your management plane. Severity scores rate bugs in isolation; attackers chain them.

If you manage FortiGates through FortiManager, patch FortiOS (7.4.10 and 7.6.5 or later on those branches, per Fortinet's advisory for older trains), and rotate every credential, pre-shared key and certificate that ever lived in FortiManager if it was exposed during the FortiJump window. Unit 42 published a YARA rule plus hunting guidance: look for anonymous 16 KB RWX memory regions inside miglogd and iked, unexpected writes to /proc//mem, and '../../' sequences in auto-script objects. A firmware update won't evict stolen secrets.

item.title: BAE Systems Incident Has Stopped U.S. Bankruptcy Notices Since October 9
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A security incident at contractor BAE Systems took the federal judiciary's Bankruptcy Noticing Center offline ten days ago, and neither BAE nor the courts has given a restoration date or said whether data was taken.
item.content:encoded:
For ten days, the federal bankruptcy system hasn't been able to tell anyone anything. The Bankruptcy Noticing Center, which produces and mails the paper and electronic notices for every U.S. bankruptcy court, went dark late on October 9 after what its operator, BAE Systems, calls a security incident.

The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts says the incident halted notice production and distribution outright. The public-facing sites are down too: bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov and the National Creditor Registration Service. BAE told reporters the problem is "isolated to the BNC system" and that it's investigating and working to restore operations.

That's about all anyone has said. Neither BAE nor the courts has described what kind of incident this is, whether ransomware is involved, or whether any data left the building. As of the latest reporting, there's no restoration date.

The silence is a problem, because the BNC isn't some back-office print shop. It handles the notices that trigger creditor meetings, filing deadlines and discharge orders, and the underlying case data includes Social Security numbers, account details and income records for people at their most financially exposed. If that data was touched, debtors are exactly the population scammers love to target.

Courts are improvising. Some judges have extended deadlines tied to notice; at least one in the Eastern District of Texas pushed active motions to stay out by 30 days. Expect more of that patchwork until the system's back.

There's a broader lesson here, too. The judiciary outsourced a single national chokepoint to a defense contractor, and when that contractor had a bad day, every bankruptcy court in the country lost its voice at once. Concentration risk doesn't show up in a vendor questionnaire until it shows up in your docket.

If you're a creditor, debtor or practitioner with an active case, don't assume silence means nothing's happening. Check the individual court's website and PACER directly for orders and deadlines, and treat any unexpected call or email about a bankruptcy case with suspicion until the courts say what, if anything, was exposed.

item.title: JPMorgan, Citi, BofA and Schwab Are Shutting AI Agents Out of Accounts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The biggest U.S. banks are blocking third-party AI agents from logging in or moving money, citing security and unresolved liability, while quietly protecting their deposit base.
item.content:encoded:
Your AI agent can book a flight. It can't move your money at most big U.S. banks, and that's now official policy rather than a technical accident.

Over the past week, the CEOs of several of the country's largest banks have said, more or less in unison, that autonomous agents stay out. Jamie Dimon used JPMorgan's third-quarter call to say the bank will limit agent access to client accounts "because you don't want rogue agents and there could be thousands of them." Citi's policy flatly bars third-party AI agents from logging into customer accounts. Bank of America is restricting agent access to consumer deposits, and Brian Moynihan told CNBC there should be "a human in the loop" to authorize money leaving an account.

Schwab is the most concrete. CEO Rick Wurster told Bloomberg the firm is actively blocking unauthorized agents from transferring client funds, and he named Meta's Muse as one of them. Schwab says it'll offer sanctioned access through MCP connections instead.

The security argument is real. Most consumer agents that "use" a bank do it the ugly way: they hold your username and password and drive the website like a human would. That's screen scraping with a language model on top, and it trains customers to hand credentials to software, which is precisely what every fraud team on earth spends its budget fighting. Add prompt injection, where a malicious web page tells the agent to do something you never asked for, and the risk isn't hypothetical.

Liability is the other unanswered question. If an agent you authorized sends $5,000 to the wrong place, who eats it: you, the bank, or the model vendor? Current consumer protection rules weren't written with a delegated bot in mind, and according to the Financial Times, regulators have privately backed the banks while officials consider whether the law needs to spell out how customers authorize autonomous software.

Now the part the press releases skip. Banks are also worried that a diligent agent would sweep every idle checking balance into the highest-yielding account it can find, every single night. That's great for you and terrible for a bank's cheap deposit funding. Blocking credential-sharing agents protects customers, and it also protects net interest margin. Both things are true.

The likely endgame is the one Schwab is pointing at: agents get in, but only through bank-issued, scoped, revocable connections where the bank sets the rules. That's safer than password sharing. It also means the banks get to decide how much freedom your agent actually has.

item.title: Two Workers Killed in Gas Explosion at Intel's Kiryat Gat Fab in Israel
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A blast during a gas delivery at Intel's Fab 28 on October 14 killed two workers and left a third in intensive care, and Intel hasn't said whether production was affected.
item.content:encoded:
Two workers are dead after an explosion at Intel's chip plant in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel, on the afternoon of October 14. A third remains hospitalized in serious condition. Magen David Adom said all three suffered severe burns, and paramedics had to resuscitate two of them at the scene.

Police say the blast appears to have been a gas cylinder malfunction during an industrial transfer. According to Israeli reporting, one delivery truck had finished unloading into the plant's tanks and disconnected, and the explosion happened while a second truck was being hooked up. Israel's Fire and Rescue Services sent hazmat teams and said the incident involved nitrogen trifluoride, a toxic gas fabs use to clean deposition chambers. Police said there's no sign of a hostile act.

One worker died that day. The second died later at Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba.

NF3 isn't flammable on its own, but it's a strong oxidizer, and it's stored and moved under high pressure. Bulk gas transfer is one of the higher-risk routine jobs at any fab, which is why it's surrounded by interlocks, procedures and hazmat training. Investigators will want to know whether the failure was the cylinder, the coupling, the procedure, or the people asked to follow it on a busy afternoon. None of that has been established yet.

Fab 28 is one of Intel's most important manufacturing sites outside the U.S., and Kiryat Gat has been the focus of a multibillion-dollar expansion. Intel hasn't said whether output was disrupted, and its upcoming third-quarter earnings call is the obvious place for analysts to ask.

The supply chain question can wait, though. Two people went to work at a chip plant and didn't come home, and the industry tends to treat fab safety as a solved problem right up until it isn't.

item.title: Cisco Email Gateway Bug Gives Root via One Attachment, and It's Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cisco says attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-76519, a CVSS 9.8 flaw that lets an unauthenticated email attachment write files and run commands as root on Secure Email Gateway appliances with File Reputation enabled.
item.content:encoded:
Your email gateway exists to open hostile attachments so your users don't have to. CVE-2026-76519 turns that job against it: a crafted attachment hits the appliance, the scanner writes attacker-chosen files to the operating system, and the attacker ends up running commands as root. No login. No user click.

Cisco published the advisory on October 14 and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation this month. The bug sits in the Advanced Malware Protection path of Secure Email Gateway, physical and virtual, and it's rated 9.8. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day and gave federal agencies until October 17 to fix it. That's a three-day window, which tells you how CISA reads the risk.

Two conditions have to be true for an appliance to be exposed. File Reputation, part of AMP, has to be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools package has to be older than 25.3.0.5525. Plenty of shops turn File Reputation on precisely because it's the feature that catches malicious attachments, so don't assume you're in the clear.

There's no workaround. Fixed AsyncOS releases are 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780, and 16.0 customers have to migrate to a fixed train. The faster route is the Content Scanner Tools update itself: 25.3.0.5525 or later contains the fix and installs without a reboot. Cisco says the hosted Secure Email Cloud Gateway is already protected and needs no customer action. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance aren't affected.

The awkward part is the timeline. The fixed AsyncOS builds shipped on September 14, and Cisco originally folded this issue into a different CVE, CVE-2026-76440. Anyone who patched on schedule last month is probably fine. Anyone who read a September advisory, decided it wasn't urgent, and parked it now has an exploited root bug on an internet-facing box. Cisco hasn't named an attacker or said how widespread the activity is.

If you run these appliances, check the Content Scanner Tools version first, update it today, then plan the AsyncOS upgrade. Then go looking. A gateway that processes every inbound message for your company is a great place for an attacker to sit and read mail, so treat an unpatched, exposed unit as a possible compromise, not just a missing patch.

item.title: Palo Alto Patches Exploited PAN-OS Management Bug CVE-2026-0322
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Palo Alto Networks fixed CVE-2026-0322, a root-level code execution flaw in the PAN-OS management interface that it says has seen very limited exploitation, and CISA wants federal agencies patched by October 17.
item.content:encoded:
Palo Alto Networks found this one itself, and by the time it did, someone was already using it. CVE-2026-0322 is a code injection bug in the PAN-OS management interface that lets an attacker run arbitrary code as root on the firewall. The October 14 advisory marks exploit maturity as "ATTACKED" and describes the activity as very limited.

There's a catch that keeps this from being a 9-plus. The attacker needs to be authenticated, with high privileges, and needs network access to the management interface. Palo Alto scores it 8.6 under CVSS 4.0 but sets its own urgency rating to the highest level, and CISA added it to the KEV catalog with an October 17 deadline. Both of those say more than the base score.

Affected gear is PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls plus Panorama, virtual and M-Series. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access aren't affected. Fixes are spread across a long list of hotfix builds on 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1 and 12.2; on the newest train you want 12.2.4, and on 11.2 the fixed builds include 11.2.13-h3 and 11.2.16, the latter due October 15. Check the advisory for your exact branch rather than guessing, because the hotfix ladder is long.

Palo Alto published three IP addresses as indicators: 66.42.72.14, 208.83.239.114 and 149.248.47.234. It hasn't said who's behind the activity or what they did once in. Threat Prevention signatures 510046 and 510047 offer partial coverage, but only with SSL decryption turned on.

"Authenticated" shouldn't make anyone relax. It means the attacker already has admin credentials, either stolen, reused or pulled from an earlier compromise, and this bug lets them go from admin console to root shell, which is a different kind of persistence. It's also the same lesson PAN-OS customers have been taught several times now. A management interface reachable from the internet, or from a flat internal network, is the real vulnerability.

Patch, then lock the management plane to a jump host or a short list of trusted internal addresses. Search your logs for those three IPs. And if admin credentials on your firewalls haven't been rotated in a while, this is a good week to do it.

item.title: XBOW Built a $250K Chrome Exploit Chain in Six Days With GPT-5.6 Sol
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: XBOW's researchers used AI agents running OpenAI's public GPT-5.6 Sol model to chain three Chrome zero-days into a full sandbox escape on Windows, earning Google's top $250,000 bounty for about $40,000 in compute.
item.content:encoded:
Six days and roughly $40,000 in API charges. That's what it took XBOW's team to go from nothing to a working Chrome full-chain exploit on Windows, the kind of attack that runs code on your machine when you load a web page. Google paid $250,000 for it, its top Chrome reward and the first full-chain payout under the program's 2026 rules.

The chain has three links. A bug in V8's Maglev compiler, where a mutable boxed number got reused during deoptimization, gave read and write access inside V8's pointer-compression cage. A flaw in Chrome's animated WebP decoder broke out of the V8 sandbox by abusing a property the sandbox doesn't enforce and Blink trusted anyway. A memory-safety overflow in Crashpad, the crash reporter, crossed the outer process sandbox. Google has fixed all three; you want Chrome 152.0.7977.82 or later, and you have to relaunch the browser for it to take.

The interesting part is who did what. XBOW says agents running OpenAI's publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol searched the Chromium source, tested hypotheses and built proof-of-concept stages. The humans picked the targets, fed the agents context, pushed back on bad results and decided which pieces to chain. The team also had to swap out part of an early chain after Google said one bug was already known.

That division of labor matters, because it lines up with what OpenAI said about this model before release. Its own evaluations found GPT-5.6 Sol could find bugs and exploitation primitives but couldn't independently produce a full chain against hardened software. XBOW didn't disprove that. It showed that a small skilled team with a public model can now do in a week what used to be a specialist project measured in months, and that the bottleneck has moved from finding primitives to knowing which ones to string together.

Most of the numbers here come from XBOW's own write-up, including the estimate that around a billion Windows Chrome users were potentially exposed. None of the bugs were exploited in the wild. Still, defenders should take the cost figure seriously. Forty thousand dollars is a rounding error for a well-funded crime group or an intelligence service, and the model is one anyone can rent.

Browser patch cadence used to be something you could let slide for a week. If AI-assisted chain building keeps getting cheaper, it's going to be less forgiving than that.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon Is Open to All Paid Users, at a Price That Doubles Dec. 1
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Google made Gemini 4 Argon broadly available on October 13 at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, which rises to $4 and $20 on December 1.
item.content:encoded:
Two weeks ago, Gemini 4 Argon was a model most people could only read about. Google kept it to cyber defenders in its Fairwind program and its own teams. As of October 13, it's broadly available to paying customers through the Gemini API, AI Studio, Antigravity, Gemini Enterprise, and the Gemini app and AI Mode for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The free API tier doesn't get it.

The pricing is the story. Through November 30, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, with cached input at $0.10. On December 1 it doubles to $4 and $20. That puts the launch price level with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, and the permanent price level with Claude Opus 5.5 and Meta's Muse Wonder. GPT-6 Astra, at $10 and $50, is still the expensive one.

Read that as a seven-week trial with a built-in price hike. It's a smart move for Google. Teams that wire Argon into a pipeline in October will have migration costs by December, and a lot of them won't bother switching back. If you're evaluating it, budget against the December number, not the one on the launch page.

Google also changed the output story. The September announcement promised up to 1 million output tokens in a response, up from 64,000. The GA notes describe a unified limit of up to 1 million input and output tokens that relies on a continuation protocol and needs API configuration, and Google hasn't clearly said how much a single uninterrupted response can hold. Third-party trackers already disagree on the default cap. Test it before you design around it.

On safety, Google says Argon hit a 0.7% attack success rate on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark over 15 adaptive attempts, and that unauthorized shortcuts on its coding evaluations dropped to 2%. Those are company-reported numbers on tests Google chose. Fairwind is also expanding to hundreds more security partners, some of whom get versions with fewer cyber restrictions for defensive work.

The benchmark picture hasn't changed since September. Argon leads on breadth and trails OpenAI on some coding tests. What changed is that developers can now check that for themselves, cheaply, for a few more weeks.

item.title: ASML Posts Record €11.7B Quarter and Says It Can't Build Enough for 2028
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: ASML reported record Q3 2026 sales of €11.7 billion and a 57.5% gross margin, and its CEO said even 30% capacity growth in 2027 and 2028 won't meet customer demand.
item.content:encoded:
The company that makes the only machines capable of printing leading-edge chips just told investors it's sold out through 2028, and the stock went down.

ASML reported third-quarter net sales of about €11.7 billion on October 14, a quarterly record and up roughly 55% from a year earlier. Gross margin came in at 57.5%, well above the range it's run in for the past couple of years. Net income was about €5.0 billion, though around €500 million of that is a paper gain from revaluing its stake in Mistral AI, so the operating picture is a bit less spectacular than the headline. It sold 17 EUV systems in the quarter, up from nine a year earlier.

Guidance is the bigger tell. ASML expects fourth-quarter sales between €14.2 billion and €15.2 billion at roughly 57% gross margin, and full-year 2026 sales of €44 billion to €45 billion. Back in January it was guiding margin in the low 50s.

CEO Christophe Fouquet said the planned capacity increases, about 30% in 2027 and another 30% in 2028, "will not allow us to meet our customer demand," and that ASML is looking at ways to add more for 2028. It didn't give a 2027 sales number and pushed long-term targets to an investor update on June 10, 2027.

Two other details are worth noting. ASML no longer reports bookings, so the closest stand-in is customer money paid or billed ahead of delivery, which rose by €5.7 billion in the quarter to €9.3 billion. That's not the same as orders, but it's hard to read as weak demand. And China fell to 23% of machine sales from 42% a year ago, a big swing in the customer mix in a single year.

Shares slipped anyway, caught in a chip sell-off driven by a hot inflation print and fears of higher rates. That's a macro story, not an ASML one. If the AI build-out slows, it'll show up in TSMC and hyperscaler capex long before it shows up in a lithography backlog that's already committed two years out.

item.title: Japan Will Fund Up to $21B in GlobalFoundries Fabs in Upstate New York
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Under the US-Japan trade deal, Japan will finance up to two new 300mm GlobalFoundries fabs in Malta, New York, with the first opening in 2029 and the US Commerce Department taking about 4% equity in the company.
item.content:encoded:
Japan is paying for America's next chip fabs. GlobalFoundries said on October 14 that it will build and run up to two new 300mm factories at its Malta, New York campus, financed with up to $21 billion from Japan under the US-Japan investment initiative.

The money comes in two pieces. Roughly $10 billion covers the first fab, which GlobalFoundries expects to break ground on later this year and bring online in 2029. Another $10 billion or so would fund a second, but that one isn't locked in; company executives said the partners will decide before the end of 2028. Each fab is rated at about 900,000 wafers a year at full output.

This is the first big chip project to come out of last year's trade deal, in which Japan pledged $550 billion of US investment in exchange for lower tariffs on its cars and other exports. The Commerce Department gets about 4% of GlobalFoundries in equity as part of the arrangement. Reuters, citing CEO Tim Breen, says that brings total government ownership to roughly 7%. The government is now a meaningful shareholder in an American foundry, which would have sounded strange two years ago.

Don't confuse this with a leading-edge play. GlobalFoundries got out of the race to the smallest transistors years ago, and the release doesn't name a process node. These fabs are for the chips everything else depends on: automotive, industrial, mixed-signal and connected infrastructure parts. GlobalFoundries named Renesas, Apple, Cirrus Logic and GM as customers, with Tokyo Electron as an equipment and technology partner. That's the supply chain that broke in 2021 and left car lots empty, and it's arguably more strategically exposed than the AI accelerators that get all the attention.

The company also says the project will create about 27,000 construction and related jobs and more than 1,000 manufacturing jobs in the Capital Region. Those numbers come from the company and should be read like any economic development pitch. A 2029 opening date is a long way out, and the second fab is still a maybe.

item.title: Microsoft Patches 1,411 Flaws, Including an Exploited MotW Bypass
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: October's Patch Tuesday fixes a record 1,411 vulnerabilities, and the one under active attack, CVE-2026-96951, lets malicious downloads skip Windows' Mark of the Web warnings.
item.content:encoded:
Fourteen hundred and eleven. That's how many vulnerabilities Microsoft fixed on October 13, and it doesn't even count the 348 it had already patched earlier in the month. For scale, SecurityWeek points out that this single release is bigger than all of Microsoft's 2025 patch output combined.

The bug that matters first is CVE-2026-96951, a security feature bypass in Windows Shell rated CVSS 8.8 and confirmed exploited in the wild. It defeats Mark of the Web, the tag Windows stamps on files that arrive from the internet. That tag is what tells SmartScreen and Office Protected View to slow down and warn you. Strip it, and a phishing attachment or a drive-by download opens like a file you made yourself.

Microsoft hasn't said who is using it or against whom. That's normal for MotW bypasses, which tend to show up as one link in a phishing chain rather than as the headline act. The flaw was reported independently by researchers at Fujitsu, Anthropic and an unnamed outside researcher, which tells you at least three separate parties tripped over the same hole.

Two more bugs were publicly disclosed before the fix. CVE-2026-108398, found by James Forshaw of Google Project Zero, bypasses Windows Defender Application Control enforcement through the .NET Framework. If WDAC is part of your allowlisting story, put that one near the top of the queue even though Microsoft rates exploitation as unlikely.
