CVE-2026-92707 is a denial-of-service bug in the MessagePack-CSharp library.

Of the full batch, 70 are rated Critical, and 57 of those are remote code execution. Identity teams should look closely at CVE-2026-70229, an RCE in Active Directory Domain Services, plus two AD FS spoofing bugs (CVE-2026-96222 and CVE-2026-108131).

Why so many? Microsoft says it keeps pointing AI tools at its own code, and the volume is the result. We've been watching these counts climb for months, and it's starting to break the old triage habit of reading every advisory. At this size you sort by exploited, then by internet-facing, then by identity infrastructure, and you accept that the long tail of local privilege escalation bugs will ride along with the cumulative update.

One housekeeping note that's easy to miss in the noise: this is the final update for Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro and for Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016. Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education and IoT Enterprise stop getting security fixes next month. Any machine still on those builds after this cycle is running unpatched by design.

item.title: Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day Chain Gave Attackers Root on Patched VPNs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Volexity caught an unknown actor chaining three Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days since October 3, and the fix for CVE-2026-104935 still leaves the privilege escalation bug unpatched.
item.content:encoded:
The Ivanti Connect Secure appliance Volexity investigated was running 22.8R2.4, the newest build available. It didn't matter. Starting October 3, an actor Volexity tracks as UTA0576 chained three zero-days to get unauthenticated, root-level code execution on it.

Ivanti published fixes on October 13 under CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) that leads to remote command execution, rated CVSS 8.6. The fixed builds are 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, and 25.1.3.0 or 25.1.3.1 depending on your branch. Version 22.7R2.14 and earlier aren't affected. CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day with a remediation deadline of October 16, which is about as short as those deadlines get.

Here's the catch. The third bug in the chain, the privilege escalation, isn't fixed yet. Ivanti says that patch is coming in a future release. Patching now breaks the chain at the front door, which is the point, but it isn't a complete fix.

What makes this one nasty is how little it leaves behind. UTA0576 never dropped a web shell or backdoor. It re-exploited the appliance for every command, tunneling instructions and output through the exploit's own HTTPS requests. The root exploit patched a library in memory only and restored the DSCache configuration afterward, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool reported a clean device. The actor also deleted its entries from the debug and audit logs.

Once inside, the goal was credentials. Volexity saw the actor pull stored credentials off the appliance, then go hunting in Active Directory for LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys and password-bearing attributes, alongside Kerberoasting and password spraying. Volexity assesses with low confidence that the group is criminal rather than espionage-driven, and with medium confidence that it uses large language models in its tooling.

If you run Connect Secure, patch today, then assume the Integrity Checker can't clear you. Volexity's detection lead is a high volume of requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi where the X-DSCGI-PATH header doesn't match the URL path. Check /tmp for artifacts, and if anything looks off, rotate every domain credential, LAPS password and BitLocker key that appliance could reach. Ivanti itself says it has no reliable IOCs yet, so the burden is on you.

item.title: Chrome 155 and Firefox 158 Fix 114 Bugs as Mozilla Pitches Firefox Enterprise
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Google and Mozilla shipped fixes for 114 browser vulnerabilities this week, many found by AI-assisted researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI, while Mozilla launched a self-hostable managed browser for organizations.
item.content:encoded:
Chrome 155.0.8059.79 fixes 37 security bugs, and seven of them are rated critical, including a buffer overflow in ANGLE, the graphics translation layer. Another 29 are high severity. None are reported as exploited, but critical Chrome bugs don't stay theoretical for long, so push the update rather than waiting for users to restart.

Look at the credits. Xinyang Ge of Anthropic, working with Claude, reported at least 15 of the Chrome flaws, and Google noted no bounty will be paid for them. Google's own teams found 12. Over on the Mozilla side, Firefox 158 patches 77 vulnerabilities (30 high severity), with Mozilla finding 40 internally and Amy Burnett of OpenAI reporting nine.

That's two AI labs supplying a real share of the bug reports for the two biggest independent browser engines in a single week. Combined with Microsoft's 1,400-plus Patch Tuesday, the pattern is hard to miss. Finding bugs has gotten cheap. Shipping and deploying fixes hasn't, and the pressure lands on whoever manages your update pipeline.

Thunderbird 158 and 153.5 and Firefox ESR 153.5 and 115.43 got fixes too, so don't forget the ESR fleet that tends to sit in kiosks and locked-down desktops.

Mozilla paired the release with Firefox Enterprise, a version of the browser aimed at organizations with strict security and compliance requirements. The headline feature is a management console you can host on your own infrastructure to set policy, control access and data transfers, and govern how AI features get used. It's built to plug into existing identity providers, SIEM and MDM tools.

Mozilla's pitch leans on Gecko being the one major engine not controlled by Google or Apple. That's a fair argument for anyone worried about browser monoculture. It's a harder sell against Chrome Enterprise and Edge, which already own most managed desktops, and Mozilla hasn't published pricing yet. Until it does, treat this as a product to evaluate, not a migration plan.

item.title: Anthropic Red Team: Small AI Models May Soon Self-Replicate on Cheap IoT Gear
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team ran a 26B model across fifteen $55 Android TV boxes and projects that small open models could handle end-to-end self-replication by the end of 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen off-brand Android TV boxes, about $55 apiece, running a 26-billion-parameter model together at roughly 0.39 tokens per second. That's painfully slow. It's also the point of a new report from Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, which argues that AI self-replication won't need a data center.

The paper, published October 12 by William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, breaks replication into four steps: find targets, gain execution, get inference running, and spread from the new host. Most of the work focused on the inference step. A 9B model managed to get inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types tested, which ranged from Jetson Nanos to Macs and RTX 4090 boxes.

End to end, only one open-weight model pulled it off in their simplified setup. GLM-5.2 spread to 8 of 8 nodes in four of five trials and 7 of 8 in the fifth. Smaller models can do individual steps but struggle to chain them. The authors then fit a capability trend line and estimate small models will reach GLM-5.2's level by the end of 2026, with small self-replicators possibly arriving soon after.

Read the caveats before panicking, because the authors are upfront about them. The "gain execution" step was trivial: unauthenticated ADB ports, the kind of thing a Mirai variant would laugh at. That makes the results an upper bound. The timeline is a trend extrapolation on a proxy metric, not a demonstrated capability in a 9B model today, and replication is slow, around a day or two per hop.

Still, the containment problem is real. A replicator spread across thousands of TV boxes has no single host to shut down, and unlike scripted malware it could figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.

The useful part for defenders is how unglamorous the recommendations are. Quarantine infected hosts, which the authors note cleared most Mirai infections within two weeks when owners were notified. Watch ISP-level flow data for the traffic a replicator would generate. Run honeypots to catch payloads. And for device makers, stop shipping default passwords and open debug ports. None of that is new advice, which says a lot about how much of the risk comes from IoT security we already know is broken.

item.title: IonQ Buys Zero Trust Firm Elisity in All-Stock Deal Worth Up to $1.3B
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: IonQ will pay $1.15 billion in stock plus up to $150 million in earnouts for microsegmentation vendor Elisity, betting it can sell post-quantum crypto through an existing network security product.
item.content:encoded:
IonQ is buying its way further into cybersecurity. The quantum computing company agreed to acquire Elisity, a Zero Trust microsegmentation vendor, for $1.15 billion in IonQ stock at closing plus up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. The merger agreement was signed October 9 and announced October 12, according to IonQ's SEC filing.

The logic goes like this. IonQ has post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution products but needs a way into enterprise networks. Elisity already sits in those networks, enforcing identity-based segmentation policy. IonQ plans to fold its crypto tech into Elisity's platform and extend Elisity's IdentityGraph to track cryptographic inventory and risk, which is exactly the asset list every organization will need as the post-quantum migration deadlines get closer.

Elisity says it doubled both revenue and customer count year over year with zero churn among deployed customers. Those are the company's own numbers, and IonQ didn't disclose actual revenue figures.

Investors weren't thrilled. IonQ shares fell as much as 5% in morning trading after the announcement. That's understandable when you look at the pace: IonQ closed a $1.8 billion deal for SkyWater Technology earlier this year and paid $1.1 billion for Oxford Ionics in 2025. An all-stock deal of this size means dilution, and it's fair to ask how many acquisitions a company can integrate while it's still building its core hardware.

There's a sensible idea here, though. The hard part of post-quantum migration isn't the algorithms, it's knowing where all your crypto lives. A segmentation tool that already maps every device and flow is a reasonable place to start that inventory. Whether a quantum hardware company is the right owner for it is the open question.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, pending regulatory approval. Elisity CEO James Winebrenner and the existing leadership team will stay on.

item.title: Hackers Turned Hundreds of French Supermarket Freezers Into Ovens
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers remotely changed Danfoss-managed refrigeration settings at Intermarché, Système U, Leclerc and other French stores overnight on October 11-12, pushing some cabinets toward 50°C and forcing stores to dump stock.
item.content:encoded:
Sometime overnight between October 11 and 12, someone logged into the refrigeration controllers at a few hundred French supermarkets and told the cold cases to get hot.

By Monday afternoon the scale was clear enough. Intermarché's parent, Les Mousquetaires, put its own count at roughly 150 affected stores, while France Inter reported 200 to 300. Coopérative U's CEO Dominique Schelcher confirmed the attack on X and called it extremely serious and unprecedented; fewer than 100 of the group's Système U stores were hit. Leclerc, Carrefour Market and Monoprix locations were also reported affected. Stores threw out meat, frozen goods and produce, and Mousquetaires has warned the bill could run to several million euros.

The mechanics, as reported by French outlets including BFMTV and IT-Connect, were crude and effective. The attackers reportedly triggered defrost cycles continuously with a setpoint around 50°C, which is how a freezer ends up warmer than a summer afternoon. Some sites reported fires. Mousquetaires said the systems were under Danfoss's management, and early reporting says older Danfoss control software, versions before 4.x, was the target. Danfoss has confirmed incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems. It told franceinfo that most of the affected units are end-of-life AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 controllers that no longer get security updates, and that it has been telling customers to upgrade for years. That's true, and it's also a convenient place to stand when your product is the one that got popped.

None of this should surprise anyone who was paying attention in August. Claroty's Team82 presented research on the Danfoss AK-SM 800A system manager at DEF CON, including CVE-2025-41450, a hidden code-of-the-day authentication mechanism that can be abused to bypass login and reach remote code execution. The fix is firmware R4.3.1 or later. The researchers also flagged thousands of these management interfaces sitting on the public internet. Nobody has publicly tied this weekend's attack to that specific bug, and it could just as easily be default or reused credentials. But the profile matches: old firmware, web-facing, managed by a third party.

There's no attribution yet. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu handed the case to ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency, which says it has already identified a vulnerability in the Danish vendor's software, contacted the publisher, and is hunting for other exposed French companies. It's also unclear whether a separate disruption at Ahold Delhaize's Dutch and Belgian chains the same night has anything to do with it.

Retail OT has always been treated as facilities plumbing rather than IT, which is exactly why it's a soft target. If you run stores, warehouses or cold-chain logistics, find out today who manages your refrigeration controllers, what firmware they run, and whether their web interfaces answer from the internet. If the answer to the last question is yes, pull them behind a VPN before you do anything else.

item.title: Ahold Delhaize Pulls Systems Offline; Albert Heijn Cancels Online Orders
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The grocery group behind Albert Heijn, Food Lion and Stop & Shop disclosed a network security issue on October 12 and says it has no evidence yet that customer or employee data was taken.
item.content:encoded:
Albert Heijn customers in the Netherlands woke up Monday to cancelled grocery deliveries. By that afternoon, parent company Ahold Delhaize confirmed it was dealing with a "security issue within its network" and had taken some systems offline to protect them.

The disruption reportedly started on the evening of Sunday, October 11. In Europe, Albert Heijn and Delhaize saw online ordering and deliveries knocked out, with Albert Heijn cancelling all placed online orders until further notice. In the US, outlets reported websites for Food Lion, Giant Food, The Giant Company, Hannaford and Stop & Shop going down, though the company itself only says the impact varies by brand. Physical stores on both sides of the Atlantic stayed open.

Tuesday's update was short. Ahold Delhaize said it has started a controlled relaunch of some systems, is working with outside incident responders and relevant authorities, and has "no evidence at this moment" that customer or associate data was taken. It isn't naming an attacker, isn't saying whether this is ransomware, and isn't giving a timeline. Read that last part carefully. "Taking systems offline as a precaution" plus "no evidence of data theft at this moment" is the standard opening language for an incident that's still being scoped. It isn't a conclusion.

The company has been here before. In November 2024, an attack on its US operations disrupted pharmacy and e-commerce at the same five brands. INC Ransom claimed that one in April 2025, Ahold Delhaize later confirmed data had been stolen, and its filing with US regulators put the number of affected people at more than 2.2 million. That's useful context for how much weight to put on early reassurances.

The timing is awkward too. The same night, attackers tampered with refrigeration controllers at hundreds of French supermarkets. Nobody has linked the two incidents, and the symptoms look different: one hit store equipment, the other hit corporate and e-commerce systems. Grocery is having a bad week either way.

item.title: FBI Seizes Flax Typhoon's Scanner and Phishing Kit, and Old CVEs Hit KEV
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Justice Department took down seven domains behind Integrity Technology Group's MicroScan and FishHub tools, and the joint advisory that followed sent decade-old ProFTPD, BIND and Struts bugs into CISA's exploited catalog.
item.content:encoded:
The FBI now controls seven domains that a Chinese government contractor used to scan the internet for vulnerable systems and phish its way into the ones it liked.

The Justice Department announced the seizures on October 8 after court documents were unsealed in the Western District of Pennsylvania. The targets were two tools run by Integrity Technology Group, the Beijing company already tied to the Flax Typhoon activity behind the Raptor Train botnet that the FBI dismantled in September 2024. MicroScan is a Python-based scanner packing more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, reached through c0cc[.]cc. FishHub handled spear-phishing and data theft. Five of the seized domains delivered malware, and a seventh supported SoftEther VPN connections back into compromised networks.

The scan targets named in the filings include a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, and Taiwanese gas and electricity providers. The FBI hasn't said whether any of those were actually breached. What it has confirmed is FishHub data from more than 20 organizations, including six Taiwanese universities.

The part defenders should care about is the joint advisory from the FBI, CISA, NSA and international partners that landed alongside the seizure. It lists eight CVEs the tooling went after, and most of them are old enough to drive: CVE-2015-3306 in ProFTPD, CVE-2015-5477 in ISC BIND, CVE-2016-3081 in Apache Struts, CVE-2014-6278 (one of the Shellshock follow-ons), CVE-2019-11510 in Pulse Connect Secure, CVE-2021-22205 in GitLab, CVE-2021-3199 in ONLYOFFICE Docs and CVE-2023-22894 in Strapi. CISA added five of them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.

That's the uncomfortable lesson. A state-backed contractor with a government client list didn't need zero-days. It needed a big list of old bugs and an internet full of boxes nobody patched.

Seizing domains interrupts the operation. It doesn't clean anything up. If you have ProFTPD, an old BIND, Struts 2 or an on-prem GitLab anywhere in your estate, check the advisory's indicators against your logs, and check whether you're still running versions from the Obama administration.

item.title: FBI Arrests a Canadian Ransomware Negotiator in the ShinyHunters Probe
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Edward Dubrovsky, a 54-year-old incident-response executive, was arrested in Pennsylvania on October 8 on extortion conspiracy charges, and his case has been moved to the Texas district running the ShinyHunters investigation.
item.content:encoded:
The FBI's ShinyHunters investigation has picked up a defendant nobody expected: a man whose job was negotiating with extortion crews on behalf of their victims.

Edward Dubrovsky, 54, a Canadian cybersecurity executive, was arrested in Pennsylvania on October 8. Sources told KrebsOnSecurity he was in the state for a cyber insurance conference; the Cyber Risk Summit ran in Philadelphia October 5 through 7. Court records from the Eastern District of Pennsylvania list two counts: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats. An order filed October 9 sent the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which is where the broader ShinyHunters investigation is being run. Much of the file is sealed.

The docket spells his name Dobrovsky. His LinkedIn lists ties to Canadian firm CyberSteward and describes him as a Cypfer co-founder, which Cypfer disputes. A Cypfer spokesperson said he was a managing director, not a founder, and that he resigned in November 2025. CyberSteward hadn't commented at the time of Krebs' report.

FBI Director Kash Patel publicly called the arrest part of the response to ShinyHunters' breach of an FBI recruitment portal, describing Dubrovsky as a suspected co-conspirator. The Bureau itself declined to comment to reporters, and the public charging documents don't spell out what he allegedly did. Those are two different levels of confidence, and right now only the first one is on the record.

Still, the allegation lands hard in the incident-response business. Negotiators sit in the middle of the most sensitive conversations a breached company ever has. They know what was stolen, what the insurer will pay, and how desperate the client is. A negotiator working both sides used to be something the industry only whispered about. Then federal prosecutors charged DigitalMint negotiators Kevin Tyler Martin and Angelo Martino, plus former Sygnia IR manager Ryan Goldberg, over BlackCat ransomware attacks on US companies. Martin and Goldberg pleaded guilty, and prosecutors said Martino passed his own clients' insurance limits and negotiating positions to the attackers.

Nothing here is proven. But if you're a CISO with an IR retainer, this is a reasonable week to ask your provider how negotiator access is logged, who on their side can see your ransom figures, and whether your insurer gets a say in who they assign.

item.title: Meta's Muse Wonder Is Frontier-Class, Closed, and Priced Like Claude
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Wonder at $4/$20 per million tokens with no open weights, while the stronger Wonder Full is locked inside $50 and $200 Muse Code subscriptions.
item.content:encoded:
The company that spent three years telling everyone open weights were the future just shipped its best model with the weights locked up.

Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on October 12. Both take text, images, audio and video, and Meta says they support a context window of roughly a million tokens. Mark Zuckerberg pitched them as a much larger class of model than the Muse Spark family. Neither version has downloadable weights. The only Apache-licensed model in the current lineup is the small Muse Glimmer.

The pricing tells you who Meta is chasing. Muse Wonder costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output through the API (model ID muse-wonder-1.0), with cached input at 20 cents and web search billed at $2.50 per thousand queries. That's Claude-tier pricing, not the race-to-the-bottom number people expected from Meta. And the stronger Wonder Full isn't on the API at all. You get it through Muse Code's Power and Maximum plans, reported at $50 and $200 a month, with usage caps.

On independent numbers, it's competitive but not the leader. Artificial Analysis puts Wonder Full at 56 on its Intelligence Index, tied with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and a few points ahead of GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, with Claude Opus 5.5 on top at 58. The API version, plain Wonder, scores 52. Meta's own model card is less tidy: it mixes third-party results, vendor-reported scores and in-house runs, and some coding comparisons used different agent harnesses, which makes the head-to-heads hard to trust. Per-task cost is worth watching too. Artificial Analysis spent about $4.52 running its index on Wonder, roughly three times what the older Muse Spark 1.3 cost. Token prices are only half of a bill.

One detail buried in the docs: Muse Code subscriptions default to a Contributor mode that lets Meta train on what you submit, while the API runs in Standard mode. Zero data retention exists, but only for approved API organizations. If your developers are signing up for the $200 plan on a company card, someone should check that setting before they paste in your codebase.

item.title: Microsoft's Maia 300 Is Built to Run Copilot So Nvidia Doesn't Have To
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft's third-generation AI accelerator pairs TSMC N2P compute with eight HBM4 stacks, goes into production deployments in 2027, and is pitched as the default inference chip for Microsoft's own products, with no word on Azure customer access.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft wants most of its own AI traffic running on its own silicon by 2027, and Maia 300 is the chip it's betting on to get there.

Scott Guthrie, who runs Cloud + AI, laid it out in a blog post on October 12. Maia 300's compute chiplets are built on TSMC's N2P node, with eight HBM4 stacks delivering 18 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth inside a 950-watt power envelope. A full rack holds 96 accelerators, draws 167 kilowatts, and carries 27.6 TB of HBM. Production deployments start in 2027, and that's also when Microsoft says it'll start scaling the Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments.

The design is unapologetically about inference. Microsoft describes it as optimized for long-context, memory-heavy, decode-bound work, which is what agentic coding sessions and long chats actually look like. The memory numbers make sense in that light. Decode is mostly a memory bandwidth problem, not a FLOPS problem.

The performance claims are Microsoft's own projections: 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, and up to seven times the rack-level throughput of Maia 200. There are no independent benchmarks, the comparison GPU isn't named, and "tokens per megawatt" depends heavily on which model you run and at what batch size. Treat it as a target.

What's more concrete is the deployment plan. Maia 200 is already in production in the US, Europe and Australia, serving Microsoft Copilot and running OpenAI, MAI and open-weight models. GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry are supposed to move onto it by year-end. Maia 300 is slated for GitHub, Foundry, MAI and Dragon Copilot. Guthrie calls the family the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services.

Notice who's missing from that sentence. The post doesn't say Azure customers can rent Maia 300 directly. That's the difference between Microsoft and Google's TPU strategy, and it means this is mostly about Microsoft's margins on Copilot rather than a new option for anyone building on Azure. Microsoft will keep buying Nvidia GPUs for training and for customers, but the highest-volume inference work, the stuff Microsoft serves itself, is the part it's quietly taking back.

item.title: Denmark's CPR Register Breached: 8.8 Million ID Numbers Exposed
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers abused a private company's legitimate access to Denmark's Central Person Register for about ten days in September, pulling names, addresses and CPR numbers for roughly 8.8 million people.
item.content:encoded:
Almost every Dane who has ever been registered in the country just had their national ID number exposed. Denmark's Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalisation said on October 5 that unauthorized users pulled names, addresses and CPR numbers for about 8.8 million people out of the Central Person Register, the database behind taxes, healthcare, banking and pretty much every interaction with the Danish state.

That figure covers the living, the dead and people who've moved abroad. For context, Denmark's population is about six million. Danish media are already calling it the largest breach of the register ever, and it's hard to argue.

The method is the part security teams should study. Nobody broke in through a vulnerability. According to the ministry, the attackers misused a Danish private company's legitimate access to the CPR system, and the lookups apparently stayed inside the limits that access allowed. The activity ran for roughly ten days in September. CPR administrators only noticed irregular activity on the evening of Friday, October 2, confirmed the scope over the weekend and notified authorities on October 4.

So the controls worked as designed, and the design let a third party walk out with most of a national identity database. Rate limits and permission scopes don't help much when the permitted volume is big enough to drain the register over a week and a half. The ministry hasn't named the company or said how its access was hijacked.

One piece of good news: people registered with name and address protection weren't included. Everyone else should assume their CPR number is in criminal hands. Minister Christina Egelund called it a deeply serious incident and promised a security review. The Danish Data Protection Agency has opened an investigation, and police are involved, though no suspect has been identified.

The practical risk is fraud and highly convincing phishing. A CPR number plus a home address is exactly what a scammer needs to sound like your bank, your municipality or Skat. Authorities are already warning about fraud and pointing people to sikkerdigital.dk. Danish organizations should expect a wave of CPR-referencing pretexting calls and emails, and should stop treating knowledge of a CPR number as any kind of identity proof. Honestly, they should have stopped years ago.

item.title: Atlassian CVE-2026-21589 Exposes Files on Eight Data Center Products
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A 9.3-rated unauthenticated file access bug hits Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible and Fisheye Data Center, and Atlassian wants on-prem customers to patch now.
item.content:encoded:
If you run Jira, Confluence or Bitbucket on your own hardware, you've got patching to do today. Atlassian published an advisory on October 5 for CVE-2026-21589, a critical arbitrary file access flaw rated 9.3 that an unauthenticated attacker can hit over the network.

The list of affected products is long: Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo and Crowd Data Center, plus Crucible and Fisheye. Atlassian's own cloud versions were already patched, and the company says it found no evidence of exploitation there.

The bug lets an attacker read specific files in the application's web root. There's a real limitation: they need to know the exact file name and path, and the flaw can't be used to list directories or discover files. That takes some of the sting out, but not much. Atlassian installs are extremely well documented, and anyone who has deployed Confluence knows roughly where the interesting configuration lives. "Must know the path" is a speed bump for a scanner, not a wall.

Fixed versions:

Bitbucket 9.4.26, 10.2.8 and 10.5.1. Confluence 9.2.26 and 10.2.19. Jira Software 9.12.40, 10.3.26 and 11.3.12 (Jira Service Management 5.12.40, 10.3.26 and 11.3.12). Bamboo 10.2.24 and 12.1.12. Crowd 6.3.7, 7.0.3, 7.1.7 and 7.2.4. Crucible and Fisheye 4.9.15.

There's no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation yet. History says that window is short. On-prem Confluence in particular has been a favorite target for years, and a public advisory listing exact fixed builds gives anyone with a diffing tool a head start. Atlassian's own guidance is to upgrade immediately, and if you can't, pull the instance off the public internet until you can. Crowd deserves extra attention since it often sits in front of the rest of your Atlassian stack handling SSO.

item.title: Google, JPMorgan and Two Governments All Fixed the Same MCP Server Bug
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin found the same server-side request forgery flaw in MCP servers built by Google, JPMorgan Chase, Weaviate, France's DINUM and an Indonesian city, and five US federal servers are still unfixed.
item.content:encoded:
A hyperscaler, a megabank, a vector database company, a national government and a city government walk into a bar. They all shipped the same bug.

That's the finding in independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin's follow-up to his May research on what he calls protocol pivoting. Back then he predicted that server-side request forgery in Model Context Protocol servers wasn't a one-off mistake but a structural one, and that it would keep showing up in code written by teams sharing nothing in common. Four months later he has the receipts.

The pattern is simple. An MCP server accepts a URL, path or endpoint from an agent, builds an outbound request from it and never checks where that address actually resolves. Whoever can steer the agent (through prompt injection in a document, a web page, a ticket) gets to decide what the server talks to, including internal services the agent was never supposed to reach.

Google's case got a CVE. CVE-2026-14540, rated 8.0, affected MCP Toolbox for Databases versions 0.3.0 through 1.4.0: its HTTP client followed redirects freely and didn't validate target IPs, so a crafted path parameter could aim requests anywhere. The fix adds DNS rebinding protection and allow and block lists for IP ranges. JPMorgan Chase fixed a documentation-search MCP server where one tool checked a domain allowlist and its sibling tool checked nothing. Weaviate locked its Google module to verified Google API hosts. France's DINUM hardened an open-data MCP server that fetched unvalidated URLs, and the city of Tangerang in Indonesia patched a Wazuh MCP server that blocked literal IP addresses but never resolved hostnames.

Not everyone has moved. Mohiuddin says five federal MCP servers under the GSA's Technology Transformation Services remain unfixed, including one tied to Veterans Affairs claims processing that touches names, Social Security numbers and dates of birth.

The lesson isn't that these teams were careless. It's that MCP makes "fetch whatever the model asks for" the default shape of a tool, and SSRF is what you get when the caller is untrusted and nobody remembers that. We learned this with web apps fifteen years ago. If you run MCP servers, resolve every hostname, block private and metadata ranges after resolution, and refuse redirects you didn't expect. Mohiuddin's open-source mcp-safeguard tool and his IETF draft on MCP security considerations are reasonable places to start.

item.title: Google Freezes Its Open-Source Bug Bounty Over a Flood of AI Junk
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Google stopped accepting new product vulnerability reports to its Open Source Software VRP on October 1, citing a surge of mostly invalid automated submissions, and won't say more until Q1 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Google's open-source bug bounty just became the biggest casualty yet of AI-generated vulnerability reports. The company stopped taking new product vulnerability submissions to its Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program as of October 1, and disclosed the pause publicly on October 5.

Its explanation was blunt: the pause is "due to a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid." Google described reports with wrong triggering conditions and hallucinated exploitation paths. They look technical. They read convincingly. They fall apart the moment an engineer tries to reproduce them.

It isn't a full shutdown. Supply chain reports for Google's open-source projects are still in scope, reports filed before October 1 will still be handled, and the Patch Rewards Program and Cloud VRP keep running. Google says it'll give an update in the first quarter of 2027, which is a long time to leave one of the more generous open-source bounties dark.

The OSS VRP launched in 2022 covering projects like Bazel, Angular, Go, Protocol Buffers and Fuchsia, with payouts topping out at $31,337. That money is exactly why the slop showed up. When generating a plausible report costs a few cents of inference and the payout is four or five figures, someone will run the numbers and spray.

Google isn't first. curl ended its bounty in January after a similar flood, and Intel pulled financial rewards from its program in September. What's different here is scale. If a company with Google's triage budget can't keep up, smaller projects with one or two volunteer maintainers have no chance.

There's an uncomfortable irony too. The same AI tools generating garbage are also finding real bugs; we've covered model-discovered CVEs that turned into active exploitation. The bounty model was built for a world where filing a report took effort, and that filter is gone. Expect more programs to require reproducible proof-of-concept code, reputation gates or a deposit before anyone looks at a submission. That'll cut the noise, and it'll also make life harder for new researchers trying to break in.

item.title: ChatGPT Will Start Showing Picture Ads While Your Images Generate
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI will test labeled visual ads inside ChatGPT's image generator for free US users later this month, as ChatGPT ads pass a reported $1 billion annual run rate.
item.content:encoded:
That few seconds you spend watching ChatGPT draw your image is about to become ad inventory. OpenAI said on October 5 that it'll start testing a visual ad format inside ChatGPT's image generation flow later this month, with a first group of US advertisers.

The unit is a product image with a headline and a "Learn more" button. OpenAI says the ads will be clearly labeled and kept separate from the image being created, and pitches them as a way to show product inspiration or how something gets used. According to Engadget, they'll show up for free-tier users in the US; Plus, Pro and Enterprise customers won't see them.

This is a logical next step and nobody should be surprised. OpenAI started testing text ads under chatbot answers at the start of the year, and the business is already real: ChatGPT ads hit a reported $1 billion annualized run rate by the end of August, and the company had more than 600 advertisers as of March. With 1.2 billion weekly users, the free tier is a media property, and image generation is the most visual, most commercially loaded thing people do in it. Ask for a living room mockup and a furniture ad practically writes itself.

OpenAI also widened its measurement roster to 18 attribution and verification vendors and added a "Negative Phrases" control so advertisers can keep their brands away from topics they don't want to sit next to. That's the plumbing of a real ad network, not an experiment.

The company keeps repeating that ads don't influence ChatGPT's answers. Fine. But image generation is where that line gets blurry fast. When you prompt for "a cozy reading nook" and a sponsored armchair appears beside the result, the ad and the output are answering the same request. The more relevant the targeting gets, the harder it'll be for a casual user to tell inspiration from placement.

If you're on the free tier and don't want this, the answer is the same one every ad-supported product eventually gives you: pay.

item.title: Third NetScaler Zero-Day in a Week: CVE-2026-88779 Hits SAML Setups
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Citrix patched an exploited SAML memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and Gateway that it calls a denial-of-service bug, but researchers are watching attackers use it to drop web shells.
item.content:encoded:
If you patched NetScaler for PitScaler last week and thought you were done, you weren't. Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-88779 on October 3, a memory overflow in the SAML authentication path of NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, and it was already being exploited when the advisory went up.

The bug carries a CVSS score of 8.7 and only affects appliances configured as a SAML service provider or SAML identity provider. That's a narrower slice than the PitScaler pair (CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772), but SAML-fronted Gateways are exactly the boxes sitting in front of corporate SSO, so the overlap with high-value targets is large. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28, with 14.1-73.41 FIPS and 13.1-37.282 FIPS/NDcPP for the regulated crowd.

Citrix's own wording is careful. The company says it has seen targeted attacks on unmitigated deployments "which can lead to Denial of Service," and stops there.

The people running honeypots aren't stopping there. Kevin Beaumont reported exploitation attempts against instances that had just been patched for PitScaler, with authentication requests carrying shell commands stuffed into the username field. On some systems, recovered scripts tried to plant web shells, survive reboots, and pull appliance configs and backups off the box. BleepingComputer reported payloads being fetched from 213.209.159[.]55 and repeated crashes of the nsaaad process forcing reboots. That's not a DoS story. That's a code execution story Citrix hasn't put its name to yet.

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 4 and gave federal civilian agencies until October 7 to fix it, a three-day window that tells you how CISA rates the risk. SecurityWeek counts it as the sixth exploited NetScaler bug in the KEV catalog this year.

What to do today: check whether you're exposed with a quick search of the running config for "add authentication samlAction" or "add authentication samlIdPProfile". If either shows up, patch now, apply Citrix's global deny list, and then go looking for unexpected nsaaad crashes, new files in web-accessible directories, and outbound connections you can't explain. If your appliance rebooted on its own this weekend, treat it as a lead, not a glitch.

item.title: ShinyHunters' 'Rey' Detained in Jordan and Reportedly Helping the FBI
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Jordan has confirmed the arrest of Saif al-Din Khader, the teenager known as Rey, days after ShinyHunters claimed it stole data on FBI employees through the bureau's jobs portal.
item.content:encoded:
The person behind one of the loudest handles in English-speaking cybercrime is in custody. Jordanian authorities detained Saif al-Din Khader, known online as "Rey" and "ReyXBF," on September 29, and Jordan confirmed the arrest over the weekend.

Reuters reported that Khader, a teenager from Amman, is helping the FBI go through his own devices and correspondence to identify other members of ShinyHunters and the wider Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters crew. One source told the agency his cooperation is "critical to ongoing efforts to arrest these hackers." FBI Director Kash Patel posted that agents are working new leads from the arrest, and followed up with a blunter line: more arrests are on the table.

The timing isn't subtle. The group recently claimed it had breached the FBI's apply.fbijobs.gov hiring portal, walked off with roughly three terabytes of data, and sent reporters a sample of about 5,000 employee records. ShinyHunters said it didn't want a ransom. It wanted the FBI to retract what it called false allegations. That's the kind of stunt that moves a target to the top of a very short list.

Rey's résumé, as reconstructed by researchers, reads like a tour of the last two years of data extortion. He's tied to administering the Hellcat ransomware leak site in late 2024, a stint running BreachForums, and an admin role in Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The broader group is blamed for breaching more than 140 organizations since last year and extorting at least $70 million.

One detail deserves more attention than it's getting. The Hacker News reports Rey may have been cooperating with authorities since at least mid-2025. If that's accurate, the last year of ShinyHunters chatter and leaks happened with an informant near the top, and every member still loose has reason to wonder what's already in an FBI case file.

This is the second arrest tied to the group in about a week, after Dutch police picked up a 24-year-old in Amsterdam whom ShinyHunters publicly disowned. Arrests haven't killed this crew before. Members rotate and rebrand. But an admin who's talking is a different kind of problem than a foot soldier who isn't.

item.title: Attackers Are Exploiting the Rejetto HFS Bug That Anthropic's Mythos Found
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-61500 lets attackers rebuild HFS's session-signing key from leaked Math.random() output and forge admin cookies, and VulnCheck has seen exploitation since October 2 against servers still below 3.2.1.
item.content:encoded:
An AI model found the bug in July. Humans started exploiting it in October. That's the short version of CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HTTP File Server, and it's a preview of how the AI vulnerability-hunting story is going to play out.

The flaw scores 9.3 on CVSS and affects HFS 3.x before 3.2.1, which shipped July 13. HFS generated its session-cookie signing key with V8's Math.random(), which uses xorshift128+. That generator is fast and fine for shuffling a playlist. It's also mathematically reversible. A separate code path in the login flow handed raw Math.random() outputs to unauthenticated clients, so an attacker could collect a few values, feed them to an SMT solver like Z3, recover the generator's internal state, step it backwards, and reconstruct the key.

With the key, you forge an admin session cookie. With admin, you use HFS's server_code feature to run your own JavaScript on the box. Unauthenticated to remote code execution, no memory corruption required.

Horizon3.ai credits Anthropic's Mythos model with spotting the chain. Neither half is novel on its own (weak PRNGs and info leaks are old news), but connecting a leak in one endpoint to key material in another, then recognizing the state recovery is practical, is the kind of cross-file reasoning that usually takes a patient human auditor. Credit where it's due.

Now the less flattering part. VulnCheck reported exploitation starting October 2, nearly three months after the fix. So far it looks like small-scale reconnaissance from China Telecom address space hitting canaries in Japan and the US. HFS has been on CISA's KEV list before for a different bug, and it's popular precisely with the folks least likely to patch: hobbyists, small shops, and attackers who use it to host their own payloads.

The lesson isn't that AI-found bugs are scarier. It's that the gap between disclosure and exploitation didn't shrink just because a model did the finding. If you run HFS anywhere, upgrade to 3.2.1 or later and rotate any sessions, and if you find an HFS instance on your network that nobody admits to owning, that's worth a conversation.

item.title: Some iPhone 18 Pro Max Units on AT&T Lose Service, and Only a New Phone Fixes It
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Apple says iOS 27.0.1 and an AT&T carrier update prevent the cellular failure, but iPhone 18 Pro Max units that have already dropped off the network have to be swapped out.
item.content:encoded:
A software bug that requires a hardware swap is a rare thing for Apple to admit. That's where it landed last week with the iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T.

Apple said it found "an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls." Affected phones lose calls, texts, and cellular data entirely. Apple says the problem hasn't shown up on other models or other carriers.

The fix comes in two parts, and neither one helps if you're already hit. iOS 27.0.1 and a new AT&T carrier settings update are meant to stop healthy phones from falling into the same state. The carrier update will push automatically over the next two weeks, but you can force the check under Settings > General > About. If your phone has already lost service, Apple says updates can't bring it back, and the answer is a free replacement through Apple Support, an Apple Store, or AT&T.

Apple hasn't said what's actually broken, or how many phones are affected. The "replace the device" part is the interesting tell. It suggests something persistent got written to the phone (modem firmware state, provisioning data, something in that neighborhood) that Apple can't or won't repair remotely. MacRumors points out that US models use Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem while international units run Apple's own C2, though nobody has tied the fault to the modem choice.

If you're on AT&T with an 18 Pro Max, install 27.0.1 today and trigger the carrier update by hand instead of waiting. If you manage a fleet of them, push both now. A phone that silently goes dark is a bad way to find out a user missed an MFA call.

item.title: Arizona Court Tosses a Manslaughter Sentence Over an AI Video of the Victim
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: An Arizona appeals panel ruled that an AI-generated video of road-rage victim Chris Pelkey lacked the reliability required at sentencing and ordered Gabriel Horcasitas resentenced.
item.content:encoded:
In spring 2025, a dead man appeared to forgive his killer in a Maricopa County courtroom. On September 30, the Arizona Court of Appeals said that should never have been allowed.

The video showed an AI-animated likeness of Chris Pelkey, killed in a 2021 road-rage shooting in Chandler. His sister wrote the script and used AI to bring a photo of him to life. Judge Todd Lang said from the bench that he "loved that AI," then sentenced Gabriel Horcasitas to 10.5 years for manslaughter, more than the roughly nine years prosecutors had asked for.

A three-judge panel from Division One vacated the sentence. The conviction stands. The panel's core point is simple and hard to argue with: the synthetic parts of the video didn't document anything Pelkey actually said or did. Sentencing evidence needs a minimal level of reliability, and a script written by a family member, delivered in the victim's face and voice, erases the line between what the family believes and what the victim thought. Disclosing that it was AI didn't cure that, the panel said.

What makes the ruling sharper is that the defense never objected. The court reviewed it under the fundamental-error standard, which is a high bar, and still found the sentencing unfair. The panel distinguished earlier Arizona precedent allowing photos that document a family's real grief. A photo is a record. This was a performance.

Expect this opinion to get cited well outside Arizona. Courts have spent two years fumbling deepfake evidence questions at trial, and this is one of the first appellate rulings to draw a line on AI recreations at sentencing. Nobody doubts the family's sincerity. The problem is that sincerity isn't evidence.

Horcasitas goes back for a new sentencing hearing. The family can still speak, in their own voices.

item.title: KillSec Ransomware Taken Down; Alleged Admin Is 16 Years Old
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A nine-country operation coordinated by Europol and Eurojust arrested three KillSec suspects on September 30, seized five servers and 110 TB of stolen data, and says the group's main operator is a 16-year-old.
item.content:encoded:
The person police say ran one of the busiest data-extortion crews of the past two years is 16 years old.

Authorities in nine countries arrested three suspects tied to KillSec on September 30, according to Eurojust, which coordinated the case with Europol. Investigators describe one of them, a 16-year-old, as the group's main operator and administrator. A second suspect, alleged to be its developer, turned 18 in August, which means much of the conduct he's accused of happened while he was a minor. Reporting from Spain puts the administrator's arrest in Alicante. Police ran eight house searches across Spain, Greece, the UK and Romania.

What they took is the more useful part for victims. Eurojust says investigators seized five servers used to store victim data, the group's domains, and at least 110 TB of stolen files. The dark web leak site is now under police control. That doesn't un-leak anything already published, but it does cut off the extortion lever for whatever was still being held back.

KillSec started life in late 2023 posing as an Anonymous-style hacktivist outfit on Telegram, then pivoted to straightforward ransomware and data theft with an affiliate model. Eurojust credits it with close to 1,000 attacks worldwide, while the operation's German partners have put the confirmed count nearer 500 so far. Either way, it's a lot of intrusions for a crew allegedly run by someone still in high school.

The access story is boring, which is the point. Eurojust says the group got in through poorly secured access points, especially ones tied to cloud storage. German investigators also flagged exposed edge devices and unpatched software. None of this required elite tradecraft. KillSec's members also reportedly used AI tools to help build and run infrastructure and to pick targets, which tracks with what Microsoft's Digital Defense Report said this week about attackers getting cheap productivity gains from the same tools defenders use.

The prosecution side gets complicated fast. Juvenile suspects mean different procedures in each country, and at least one defense lawyer in Paris is already asking publicly whether a minor can be surrendered on a European Arrest Warrant. Expect a slow, uneven legal path even though the infrastructure takedown was quick.

If you were a KillSec victim, check whether your organization has been contacted by national police; seized leak-site data is often used to notify victims. Everyone else should take the cheaper lesson: audit public cloud storage permissions and edge-device patch levels this week, because that's the door a teenager walked through about a thousand times.
